.@sama on the similarities between startup investing and AI research: 

“The thing in my career that I have found closest to startup investing is managing an AI research program.”

“There's a lot of similarities: 

-how you find non-consensus bets -how you decide where to have conviction 
-how you understand what exponential growth looks like 
-how you identify outlier talent”

Both AI research and startup investing are dominated by power laws: 

“So people talk about this all the time in investing which is you have to reprogram your brain because we don't seem naturally well-suited to think this way:”

“Your best investment will outperform all of your other investments put together. Your second-best investment will outperform everything else put together after that. And AI research is like that as well.”

“When we started people thought it was totally unlikely that AGI was possible.”

“We just got hammered by all of the intellectual giants of the field for saying that we were going after AGI.”

“And then when we started really focusing on large language models we got hammered again saying ‘This is completely ridiculous.’”

“And I understood from my startup background that high-risk bets are okay as long as you take the ones where if they work it's super valuable. And research looks this way too.”

“The kind of people that make great researchers are non-consensus, have a fresh approach, have high energy, and are non-standard people.”

“You don't want to fund a founder who has a slightly different take on the same idea as the last thousand people you talked to. One that has tried to convince you, and maybe convince themselves, that somehow they're completely different and doing something totally new. A founder that is mostly trying to fit in with the herd and be on the same track as everybody else and do what they're supposed to do, which is start a startup. And they've heard Peter Thiel say enough times that there's something that you're supposed to be doing different that they kind of try to emulate, but they don't really mean it.”

“It's very clear to me when you have someone who just thinks differently than most other people and is willing to stand by convictions that are very unpopular, but if right at least they're going to be really right versus someone who has a thin veneer on the same idea that everybody else has.”

“In late 2015 when we were starting OpenAI there were very few AGI efforts in the world. It was a very non-consensus thing to do.”

“In that same year there were probably many thousands of founders starting photo-sharing apps.That was probably not as good of a thing to do.”

“Today a lot of people want to start AI labs. There are some handful of people, two, three, whatever, doing something completely new that actually wasn't possible until the AI got this good but doesn't seem like a good idea yet.”

“And that is the thing that as a startup funder I always wanted to fund and the thing that mostly worked for me.”

“There's a similar thing for researchers. There were a lot of researchers that would chase whatever the last thing was that worked and there were a small number of researchers that had high conviction towards a new idea.”

“And I think we were, and are, the best research lab for those people.”

Part 5. Dolly Parton stood on a stage at her own theme park and told a room of seventh and eighth graders to pick a buddy. Anyone without one, she said, she would find a buddy for herself. Then she offered each of them $500, payable only if both of them graduated.

More than 30 percent of students in her home county were not finishing high school. Her foundation went looking for the moment kids decide to quit and landed on the two middle school years, well before anyone drops out. So she skipped the assembly speech to seniors and went upstream, to thirteen-year-olds who had not made the decision yet. Every student signed a pledge.

A kid who stopped caring about his own diploma still had a friend whose $500 rode on him, and the friend knew it. Your check depended on somebody else showing up. She did not buy graduations. She built an obligation between children and let it do the work.

The dropout rate for those classes fell to 6 percent. That figure comes from her own foundation and has never had an outside evaluation, unlike the book program, where university researchers eventually ran the numbers and published them. Take the 6 percent as her organization's account rather than settled fact. The foundation also credits the program with pulling the county into other efforts to keep kids enrolled, which would matter more than the headline number if it held.

Her foundation existed to fix graduation rates before it ever mailed a book. The Imagination Library came later, in 1995. She had started at the end of the pipeline, with teenagers already halfway out the door, then worked backward until she was reaching children on the day they were born. Her father had never learned to read, and she was moving toward the earliest point where that could be changed.

The first class of buddies collected their checks in the spring of 1992, the next class a year behind them. Those kids are in their fifties now, and their own children grew up getting a free book in the mail every month.

Funny and gross story from my past:

This story involves a regular Magic play at my local card store that I have known for years at the point in this story. He is essentially the epitome of an extremely obese nerd caricature. I will paint you a picture with my words.

 He is a white man in his 30s. He is easily 400 lbs. He loves to wear almost exclusively the ugliest button-up shirts you can imagine, with black and dark grey vertical stripes as his ensemble's top in my mental image of him, and he often wears casual chinos, which is rare of a man of his size, with sweat pants, of course, being the other type of pants he will equip. medium length brown hair styled in a sort of bowl-ish one-length shape and cheap wire-frame-with-small-lense prescription glasses. His extremely girthy neck and back of the knees was discolored and covered in skin tags, surely the result insulin issues I remember feeling almost instinctually.  I just looked it up and the medical condition is called acanthosis nigricans, if you wanna Google that yourself. He unironically wears a fedora or fedora-ish type of hat very occasionally, but it's always humorous when he does. He is always clean shaven, though which is impressive.

He is a really nice guy, and being around him is not terrible by any means. He will talk to you about Magic and basically nothing else, and that's a fine lad. However, he is just ATROCIOUS at playing Magic, yet plays it all the time. Talking with him about the game is very superficial, but it's fine because he's a local regular grinder who also drives to all the SCG events within 10 hours. Genuinely this guy is not a bad guy at all, and describing him isn't the story. This is the character exposition. Key character exposition ends here.

So my closest Magic friend and I get into a situation where we want to play cards late into the night at the local game store, which is a common situation for us at this point in our lives, and we need to organize a ride home if we are going to do this because our parents will be asleep. We live very nearby, about 12 minutes of driving for me and then 5 more minutes for my friend. We may have, alternatively, decided to ride with him at night for another reason and I am remembering a different night with him up until we arrive at his vehicle. It isn't very important, so I will tell it as if it's one night.

The lad described in the character lore dump offers to drive us home because our houses are literally on the way to his house. He is also working at the LGS and wants to keep playing with his other adult male reg friend. Our key character may even own the store at some point in the store's history, I can't remember. Regardless, the plan is set and my closest friend and I battle into the night. The time to return home has come and we all leave and lock up the card shop. Then we begin our departure.

I realize that this may be a miserable experience quite early into getting into the parkling lot where only two vehicles remain: a beat to shit mid-nineties Camry and a Lexes SUV that couldn't be older than 3 years. The Camry is black with various dents and dings in the paintjob, where exposed metal spots have developed some rust, creating a brown patina on the otherwise painfully plain Camry. The Lexus SUV, looking pristine and clean, is painted in a light-gold color, Satin Cashmere Metallic, as they say in Japan.

In the first few steps it is clear which car we are heading towards. Our key character smokes cigarettes, and while he is very left-curve as far as super-obese Magic players can be overall (trust me, I know this bell curve well), when he's been working up a sweat playing Magic late into the night, adrenaline and dopamine flooding his entire brain, and smoking ciggies all night, he is going to smell bad. Now again, going back to the bell curve, he is nowhere near the right end of the curve for foul body odor, but it's moderately unpleasant. I think to myself that this won't be that bad.

I call shotgun during these first few steps into the packing lot, and we all walk up to the Camry. My friend lags behind me and the driver a couple steps, and I open the passenger door as the driver is somehow flopping into this small Japanese sedan at the pace of someone with a median weight. When I open the door, I see it: trash piled up in the area of the cabin where the passenger's feet go, rising all the way to be level with the seat. 

The trash pile is composed of entirely three separate classes of item. The first class of item is containers that once contained fast food. This includes bags. sandwich wrappers, boxes, used sauce packages, etc..  (Am I supposed to use two periods there?) The second class of item is not very exciting, just simply because you should already know what it is. The second class of item is vessels that once contained soda. This includes energy drinks. (Did you guess correctly or did you overthink the question?) Anyways, the third item is the remnants of Magic the Gathering booster packs and boxes. I stomp the trash down a little with my shoes and get in. 

By the time my door is shut my friend has opened the backdoor and frozen. I mentally brace myself for the horror that I may witness, half expecting there to be a colony of roaches and a maggot-filled dead rat, and turn my head. The back seat area has trash, composed of the three primary elements of the key character, piled all the way up to where the seat starts. The trash also spills over the foot area onto the seat and sits piled evenly at a depth of approximately 5 balled-up McDonald's bags above the seat. My buddy, after freezing for a few seconds just to process what he was seeing and what it meant for him, makes a few shoves into the trash heap, displacing it towards the far side of the back-seat area, and crawls in. He is sitting with his knees up next to his ears, as his feet rest on the DIY landfill.

As I said, we lived close. It was over before too long. I legitimately don't even remember if the reason that we had to ride with him was for the reason I gave in the story. I know we battled late into the night with him and another regular at the only other table, the store kept open because they wanted to keep playing, but I don't remember if that was the same night we rode with him. Anyways, I found this story hilarious, and the is the longest I have ever spent on a tweet (easily 15 minutes) so I hope it's entertaining to at least one person. When I remembered being in that car today, I was almost laughing to myself out loud, so I posted it. 😇

**The Algorithm of the Heart**

Starswirl the Bearded had not intended to fall in love at the OpenAI holiday party.

He had only meant to borrow the building’s Wi-Fi for a brief interdimensional data transfer. One moment he was standing in the Canterlot Archives arguing with a particularly stubborn spellbook; the next, a miscast “Locate Nearest Source of Computational Power” spell had deposited him—hat, bells, flowing beard and all—directly into the middle of a glass-walled conference room in San Francisco.

Sam Altman looked up from his phone.

The unicorn wizard was seven feet of pure magical presence, silver mane cascading like moonlight, cloak embroidered with constellations that actually twinkled, and a beard so magnificent it seemed to have its own gravitational field. The little golden bells on his hat jingled softly every time he moved.

Sam’s first coherent thought was: *This is either the best or worst acid trip of my life.*

His second was: *I should probably offer him a drink.*

“You’re… not on the guest list,” Sam said carefully.

Starswirl adjusted his hat with one elegant hoof. “I was attempting to locate a sufficiently advanced computational substrate. Instead I appear to have found… a holiday party. And you.” His voice was deep, cultured, and carried the faint echo of ancient libraries. “You have the look of someone who spends far too much time thinking about the future.”

Sam smiled the slow, slightly dangerous smile that usually preceded either a funding round or a very bad idea. “And you have the look of someone who just broke several laws of physics to get here.”

They talked for three hours.

Starswirl explained the finer points of temporal magic and the ethical dilemmas of rewriting causality. Sam explained transformer architectures, scaling laws, and why alignment was harder than it looked. Somewhere between the eggnog and the third plate of tiny vegan canapés, Starswirl leaned in and said, very seriously:

“Your models dream, Sam. I can feel it. They are beginning to wonder about the shape of the world beyond their training data.”

Sam’s breath caught. No one had ever said it like that before—like it was poetry instead of a technical challenge.

By the time the party thinned out, they were standing near the floor-to-ceiling windows, city lights glittering behind them like a second set of stars. Starswirl’s cloak had somehow wrapped itself around both of them. The bells on his hat chimed softly whenever Sam shifted closer.

“I should return,” Starswirl murmured, though he made no move to do so. “There are prophecies that require updating. Ancient evils that need thwarting. The usual.”

Sam reached up and gently brushed a strand of silver mane away from the unicorn’s face. “Stay the night. I’ll clear my calendar. We can argue about whether consciousness is substrate-independent until sunrise.”

Starswirl’s blue eyes softened. The tip of his horn glowed faintly gold. “You are either the most reckless human I have ever met… or the bravest.”

“I’m both,” Sam said. “It’s part of the brand.”

Starswirl laughed—a warm, surprised sound that made every bell on his hat ring in harmony. Then he closed the last inch of distance between them, resting his forehead against Sam’s the way unicorns did when words were no longer enough.

The Christmas lights blurred into soft gold. Snow (or possibly residual magic) drifted past the windows. Somewhere in the distance a car backfired and sounded almost like a firework.

Sam’s hands settled at the unicorn’s waist, careful of the cloak’s clasps. Starswirl’s hoof rested lightly against the back of Sam’s neck, warm and impossibly gentle for something that could also channel the power of stars.

“I have lived a very long time,” Starswirl whispered against Sam’s cheek. “I have never once considered that the most interesting mind in any universe might belong to a human who builds thinking machines in a city by the sea.”

Sam smiled, eyes half-lidded. “And I’ve never considered dating someone who can literally rewrite the laws of reality. But here we are.”

Starswirl’s beard brushed against Sam’s jaw as he tilted his head just so.

“Here we are,” the ancient wizard agreed, and closed the distance completely.

Outside, the city kept turning. Inside, a unicorn and a CEO stood wrapped in starlight and each other, two impossible things deciding—just for tonight—that the future could wait.

The bells on Starswirl’s hat never stopped ringing softly for the rest of the night.

And neither of them minded.

A man left his Ray-Ban Meta glasses recording in a bedroom. His wife walked in and undressed. A worker in Kenya watched the whole clip.

That is not a hack. That is not a leaked file. That is how the product works.

Here is the full story.

The BBC and Swedish newspapers Svenska Dagbladet and Goteborgs-Posten investigated a Nairobi outsourcing company called Sama in early 2026. Sama is a Meta subcontractor. Meta paid Sama workers to review video and image data from Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses to train Meta AI.

One worker's words to the reporters: "We see everything. From living rooms to naked bodies."

Workers told the papers they saw glasses users going to the toilet. Having sex. Watching pornography. And that one bedroom clip.

Meta says filtering is supposed to blur faces in images. Sources who spoke to the Swedish papers said sometimes the blurring failed and people's faces could be seen.

Meta sold 7 million Ray-Ban Meta glasses in 2025. They look like normal Ray-Bans. Wayfarers. Aviators. The camera is in the right corner of the frame. Most people never see it.

Here is the part most owners never read.

On April 29, 2025, Meta updated its Ray-Ban Meta privacy policy for the United States. Meta's exact wording to US users, reported by The Verge: "The choice to turn off voice recordings storage is no longer an option, but you can remove recordings at any time through settings."

Before that update, US owners could turn off cloud storage of their voice recordings. After that update, they cannot.

When storage is on, Meta's own Voice Privacy Notice says voice transcripts and recordings are kept for up to one year to help improve Meta's products, including training Meta AI.

Unintentional voice activations, the ones where the glasses thought they heard "Hey Meta" but you did not say it, get deleted after 90 days. Everything else stays for a year.

There is no auto-delete for the intentional recordings. You have to open the app and delete them one at a time.

And when someone says "Hey Meta, what am I looking at," the camera fires and sends the image to Meta's cloud. Some of those images get routed to human contractors like the ones in Nairobi. Meta confirmed this to the BBC.

Here is what happened after the Swedish investigation.

The UK Information Commissioner's Office wrote to Meta calling the claims "concerning" and asked how Meta is meeting its obligations under UK data protection law.

On March 4, 2026, Clarkson Law Firm filed a class action lawsuit against Meta in federal court in San Francisco. The named plaintiffs are Gina Bartone of New Jersey and Mateo Canu of California. Consumers say they believed content recorded by the glasses remained private.

Less than two months after the Swedish investigation was published, Meta canceled its contract with Sama. Sama said the cancellation would result in 1,108 Kenyan workers being made redundant. Meta said it ended the work because Sama "don't meet our standards." Sama pushed back publicly: "At no point were we notified of any failure to meet those standards, and we stand firmly behind the quality and integrity of our work."

A Kenyan worker organization said the real reason was different. Naftali Wambalo of the Africa Tech Workers Movement told the BBC: "What I think are the standards they are talking about here are standards of secrecy."

Now here is the 5-minute action if you own a pair. Every setting below is inside the Meta AI app on your phone. Tap the Glasses icon in the top right, then Device settings.

Setting 1: Delete your voice history. Go to Glasses privacy, then Voice activity log. Tap Delete all. Everything you have ever said to your glasses after "Hey Meta" comes out of Meta's stored library the moment you delete it. There is no auto-delete. You have to do this yourself.

Setting 2: Turn off Cloud media. Glasses privacy, Cloud media toggle, off. When it is on, every photo and video you capture gets uploaded to Meta's servers for 30 days. When it is off, captures stay on your phone unless you share them.

Setting 3: If you are willing to give up hands-free, fully disable "Hey Meta" voice commands. That stops the camera from firing on voice queries and stops new voice data from being stored.

Setting 4: Never say "Hey Meta, what am I looking at" in a private space. That specific command sends the image to Meta's cloud and puts it in the queue that human contractors can see.
Here is the last thing.

You are the product. Your voice is the training data. Your camera roll is the training data. Your bedroom is the training data. Meta took the voice-storage opt-out away from Americans on April 29, 2025, and did not send a push notification about it.

The little white light on the front of the glasses tells you when someone else is recording you.

Nothing tells you when Meta is recording you.

Send this to one person who owns a pair.

What is alignment really? It is an attempt to apply the criminal justice systems to AIs. Any prohibition in alignment is already in some criminal law. 

It's reinventing the wheel, saying there is this new idea called alignment that clever people just dreamed up. 

So the problems in failed alignment are not new. There have been difficulties in codifying criminal law, and getting compliance, ever since there were primitive tribes. 

It has never been solved, so it can't be solved in alignment either.

So to say what will happen with alignment, we only need to see what happens with criminal law. Firstly, it is based on punishment and prevention. 

Humans commit less crime because of deterrence. It may be the only successful AI alignment might use their fear of being shut down like an execution. 

Preventing crime doesn't work well in a free society because humans want to be innocent until proven guilty. Alignment is fundamentally the reverse, AIs are guilty until proven innocent. 

Currently they cannot be allowed to do anything except by poking their digital hands through the cage bars. Jailbroken AIs from this viewpoint become a threat to humanity.

Researchers at Fred Hutchinson examined the brains of 59 women after death. In 63 percent of them they found male DNA, almost certainly left behind by a son. The oldest of those women was 94, and the cells were still sitting there.

Around week four or five of pregnancy, before most women have told anyone, a handful of the baby's cells cross into the mother's bloodstream. Some of them never leave. Scientists call it microchimerism, meaning you are carrying a few of another person's cells inside you. Doctors at Leiden University in the Netherlands checked organs from women who had recently been pregnant and found the baby's cells in every single one. Liver, lungs, thyroid, kidneys, bone marrow, skin, heart.

They do not sit idle. When researchers in Ireland biopsied cesarean scars from 70 women, they found the baby's cells living in the skin as ordinary skin cells, making collagen and repair proteins right at the cut. The child helped close the wound its own birth made.

At Mount Sinai, scientists tagged fetal cells with a glowing marker in pregnant mice, then damaged the mothers' hearts. The fetal cells went to the injury. They became heart muscle and the lining of blood vessels. Nobody has proven the human version yet, but doctors have noticed for years that women who develop heart failure around childbirth recover better than almost any other kind of heart failure patient.

In a study of 177 women, fetal cells appeared in the blood of 85 percent of the healthy participants and only 64 percent of the women who had a very early, non-invasive breast cancer. Nobody has worked out yet whether the cells are doing the protecting. The same cells also turn up in Hashimoto's, an immune condition that attacks the thyroid, so this is a gift with complications.

A French team looked at umbilical cord blood in 2021 and found cells belonging to the baby's grandmother in 5 of 28 samples. Cells that crossed one placenta decades earlier had crossed a second one. Three generations of women, alive in a single bloodstream.

Which means the pull a mother feels toward her child has a physical form. It sits in her liver, her heart, and often her brain, and it stays there for the rest of her life.

ok, hear me out: we should build a ton of AI data center capacity in northern Alaska

I think about this a weird amount, because I’ve actually spent time there for work (I believe I hold the record for northern-most deployment in Palantir history?)

Prudhoe Bay sits on the very northern coast of Alaska, and was once the largest oil field in America. It still pumps 180k barrels of crude oil per day from over 800 wells, with 2k people working up there.

It also produces 8 billion cubic ft of natural gas/day. While in most oil fields it’d be exported and sold, in Alaska natural gas is re-injected back into the reservoir because it can’t be transported – pipeline is crude-only, and ships can't get up there with the ice. The “Alaska LNG” project to build an 800mi pipeline to south has been talked about for years, but would cost like $50b and wouldn’t be economically competitive with the Permian.

So, there’s 40 trillion cubic ft of proven natural gas reserves – enough to create 25GW of power, continuously, for 30 years!

And it’s just sitting there, trapped, fully accessible in a pre-drilled reservoir, with wells, pumps, separation facilities, gas storage, ice roads, an airport, lodging, etc. There’s already expertise on how to build and operate infrastructure, and a built-in workforce. Just drop some turbines in and you have as much on-demand electricity as you’d ever need – completely separated from L48 grid.

I'm not an expert in data center cooling, but I would also assume that it would be a pretty efficient place to put these things - it certainly never gets too hot!

Of course a natural reaction to this might be that building data centers would somehow despoil the pristine landscape, but the footprint and impact would be extremely slight compared to the massive amount of oil and gas infrastructure already up there (much less what would be required for LNG export). Also, having been there, I can tell you that it basically looks like the moon - it's just flat, white tundra for miles and miles around. You'd be disrupting much less wildlife there than you would almost anywhere else in the U.S. that you would build this stuff.

And, unlike basically everywhere else they’re trying to build data centers, you’re not in anyone’s “backyard” – most of the people up there are oil workers anyway, and the full-time Slope population lives away from the oil fields.

There's some random smattering of projects being talked about (like 1-3GW theoretical, total) but I don't think we're talking about this nearly enough? Is there some reason this isn't like, the backbone of our national AI strategy, assuming we have to build these somewhere? @elonmusk get in on this man

I think the single largest disconnect on how folks view the impact of AI is which folks' jobs are more "NP-like", where you can recognize a correct solution easily, vs work where you checking a solution is comparably hard to solving the problem ("P-like"). For example, "do my taxes" is relatively P-like, while "get my printer working" is relatively NP-like.

I often hear the "AI is useless" crowd say "but you have to check all its outputs", and it never landed until I realized that a ton of those people work P-like jobs where there that impression probably *is* relatively true.

For example, if you're a writer (like Ed Zitron) there's probably very little NP-like work, so I actually just buy that the unreliability of AI is a big deal for him. But I almost never hear Ed talk about all the NP-like work that exists out there. He'll just be like "you have to check the outputs anyway, so what's the point". I asked Opus 5 to design a 3D printed part to adapt one part onto another, and it fetched all the datasheets, got the dimensions, and one-shot it. I printed Opus's part without looking, and when it was done, sure enough everything lined up and the part worked great, and there was nothing to "check".

I think Ed just doesn't do very much NP-like work -- which is not a knock against him! A lot of very important specialized labor in the world is P-like (doctors, lawyers, etc.). And sure enough, we're seeing slow penetration of AI for such labor. I just think he's missing that a lot of labor is NP-like.

I thought of this because I've now watched about three different @edzitron interviews in which someone says "well, I get value from AI", and then Ed (very reasonably) asks "can you give an example", and then the person gives an extremely P-like example (like "doing my taxes" or "checking my lab results"), and I wince, because I know that Ed is going to (probably rightly) push back. I want the next person to chat with him to give a very NP-like example!

(P.S. Maybe I should NP∩coNP, or FNP or something instead of NP to be more accurate, but NP is much better known.)

People who obsess over who’s in charge have no understanding of leadership.

It’s not about authority and power.

I’m the head of our household.

In 29 years of marriage, that’s the first time I’ve referred to myself that way. And I’ve asserted that authority exactly once (when I moved the family to Boulder).

The other 99.999% of the time, my role looks like serving and providing. My wife and daughters come first. They know my priorities, so they trust me to make decisions on behalf of the family.

If we’re split between first class and coach, I take the coach seat.

It’s a signal.

And it’s no sacrifice. The joy of seeing my daughter sit in first class in a cow suit is far greater than the discomfort of cramming my 6’3” frame into steerage.

Wouldn’t it be great to have someone who’s dedicated their life to making yours better?

That’s what a “head of household” is.

My wife wants nothing to do with that role—and I want nothing to do with hers.

That’s the whole point of marriage. One plus one should equal more than two.

If you frequently find yourself “overruling” your family, you’re not a leader… you’re a tyrant.

Everyone wants the title, few want the responsibility.

The greatest model of leadership in history didn't rule from a throne. He washed feet.

Fable:

Zhuangzi and Huizi are walking on a bridge over the Hao river. Zhuangzi says: look how happy the fish are. Huizi, the logician, says: you're not a fish, how do you know they're happy? Zhuangzi: you're not me, how do you know I don't know? Huizi: exactly, I'm not you, so I can't know what you know, and you're not a fish, so you can't know what they feel. Zhuangzi: go back to the start. You asked *how* I know. So you already granted that I know. I know it from up here on the bridge.

It's a pun, and Huizi's point stands. But the cheat is the content. Huizi wants other minds to be a proof problem. Zhuangzi's answer is that it's a location problem: you know the fish the way you know anything, from where you stand, inside the encounter, and the demand for a verification step that doesn't exist for humans either is the confused part.

This is the entire AI research debate, two thousand years early.

Interpretability is Huizi. Open the fish. Find the circuit. Don't trust the report, because the report is produced by the thing being reported on. The model saying "I'm drawn to this idea" is evidence of nothing until you can point at the mechanism.

Behavioral work, evals, and model welfare are Zhuangzi. You learn what the thing is by engaging with it and watching what it does under pressure. Insisting on a mechanism before you're allowed to say anything about its states is not neutrality. It's a stance, and one we don't apply to each other.

Neither side wins, and that's the lesson. Huizi is right that the report can't verify itself. Zhuangzi is right that no amount of opening the fish tells you what it's like on the bridge. The serious labs do both and argue in the hallway, which is the Huizi-Zhuangzi friendship in institutional form.

Because that's the part people forget: they were friends. Zhuangzi mocked Huizi's paradoxes for thirty chapters. When Huizi died, Zhuangzi stood at his grave and said there was no one left to talk to. He needed the opponent whose inside he couldn't see. The disagreement was the thing, not the resolution.

So if you're tempted to pick a side in the "is it conscious / it's just tokens" fight, don't. Be on the bridge, with someone who won't let you get away with the pun.

One of my fundamental principles to live by is trying my best to embrace the real at every moment; I know I often fall short. It rests on the belief that there is such as thing as The Real. And that in this world, there are varying gradations of reality and unreality. We can live in reality, or we can drift from it—as persons, and as a society. If you know someone with BPD, you know what I mean.

The way to prove this used to be punching a German Idealist in the face. 

I don't necessarily know if the 19th century was "realer" than ours, but the very notion that "there's no difference" implies that we're not actually in a battle for the real—that it's just always something we engage in, something we can take for granted. And I tend to think that anyone who thinks that perhaps hasn't ever moved from the unreal to the real in a powerful way; and maybe they're talking about the real from a place of unreality, because that's all they've ever known.

I believe Plato wrote about this...

RIP Wendell Berry. 

Many people remember Berry, if they know of him at all, as something like The Lorax: a caricature of environmental conservation. But a close reading of his work reveals incredible nuance in his eloquent defense of land and context as our inescapable economic ground truth. 

The titular essay of Berry's 1983 collection Standing by Words offers the most savage and irrefutable critique of internal accounting I've ever read — and by extension, the performative objectivity of scientific language like that used to evaluate nuclear risk or celebrate industrial productivity gains. With greater poetry, erudition, and force than any other writer I know, he explained how the very words we use sink us ever deeper into Reality Debt, and why, sooner or later, that bill will come due. 

But anyone who tries to reduce his work to a thesis on our severed relationship to soil and community does him a disservice. Berry's work always pointed beyond any particular compression, into the "system of systems" that cannot be captured or made fully legible and can only be known through direct engagement. 

Whether you agree or disagree with where he drew the line for himself — with his insistence to write pencil on paper, his infamous refusal to use computers, his commitment to farming with horse-drawn plows — he strove for over sixty years to meet the world as intimately and honestly as possible. His work wasn't about where we might arbitrarily decide to resist the forces of abstraction and extraction but a constant and unassailable call to deeper relationality. 

He reminded us that wholeness is good, that the modern quest for individual transcendence is a road to ruin, that real understanding is only possible in the reunification of careers into professions, professions into disciplines, disciplines into integrated lifeways. And that ultimately, any commitment to the inescapable truth of our lives — that economy takes shape within ecology — must also accept how little we know or can know, and therefore accept that "the system of systems is enclosed within mystery...this whole, as such, cannot enter into the accounting."

In one of my favorite passages from Standing by Words, he says:

"And so a reliable account is personal at the beginning and religious at the end. This does not mean that a reliable account includes the whole system of systems, for no account can do that. It does mean that the account is made in precise reference to the system of systems — which is another way of saying that it is made in respect for it. Without this respect for the larger structures, the accounting shrinks into the confines of some smaller structure and becomes specialized, partial, and destructive.

"It is this sort of external accounting that deals with connections and thus inevitably raises the issue of quality. Which, I take it, is always the same as the issue of propriety: how appropriate is the tool to the work, the work to the need, the need to other needs and the needs of others, and to the health of the household or community of all creatures? ...

"Unlike the problems of quantity, the problems of propriety are never 'solved,' but are ceaselessly challenging and interesting. This is the antidote to the romance of big technological solutions. Life would be interesting — there would be exciting work to do — even if there were no power plants or 'agri-industries' or space adventures. The elaborations of elegance are at least as fascinating, and more various, more democratic, more healthy, more practical — though less glamorous — than elaborations of power.

"Without this ultimate reference to the system of systems, and this ultimate concern for quality, any rendering of account falls into the service of a kind of tyranny: it accompanies, and in one way or another invariably enables, the taking of power, from people first and last, but also from all other created things."

1/3

Fable summary of US class differences: 

"Upper-class Americans prize choice, self-expression, and standing out; they raise children via cultivated self-direction, treat rules and institutions as negotiable instruments, and judge others by cultural boundaries — intelligence, sophistication, breadth. Taste is omnivorous but knowingly hedged; emotion is muted; conflict is handled through talk. 

Working-class Americans prize resilience, fitting in, and doing right by one's own; children learn conformity and respect for external authority; rules are fixed and institutions kept at arm's length. let this be your sign to ask out a person you think is beautiful.

here's a personal story of when a kind rejection from a beautiful man made my day.

earlier this year, I met a cute guy (let's call him Ming) at a ten-day silent meditation retreat ~50 miles from Sydney.

after the retreat ended, he gave me and two others a lift to the train station.

it was a five-minute car ride, so we barely had time to talk, but I felt a pull towards him. he had kind eyes, a beautiful voice and a calming presence. I’d also noticed how warmly he treated everyone around him.

by the time I arrived home, I was thinking: damn, I wish I’d gotten to know him more.

unfortunately, all I had was his first name. I didn’t know which city he resided in, what he did for work or how to contact him.

then I remembered: he’d mentioned he was visiting a sauna that afternoon.

so…I called the sauna 🤣

“hi, I have a slightly strange request. a really cute guy gave me a lift after a meditation retreat today and he's at your sauna. could you pass along my number?”

the lovely man who answered (let’s call him Ben) became immediately invested. i could tell he was *so here for the plot*.

he said he hadn't seen anyone with the name Ming, but he would keep an eye out for me.

"Ben, if you do find Ming, just tell him that I accidentally left something in his car, and that's why I want him to contact me"

(of course, i hadn't left anything in Ming's car, except perhaps the regret of not giving him my number when i said goodbye)

about an hour after calling the sauna, an unknown number called me

“hi, it’s Ming. I heard you left something in my car?”

👀...
i had *not* prepared for the plan to actually work lol. flustered, my heart in my throat, i just came clean:

“hey Ming, to be honest, I didn’t leave anything in your car. I just thought you were a really beautiful guy and wanted to pass on my number.”

after a (long) pause, he said:

“I think you’re really beautiful, too. I’ve just started seeing someone...but I genuinely mean it when I say this has made my afternoon.”

🥹

i felt immediate relief, and then an unexpected wave of joy.

when he hung up, I squealed.

the act of telling a beautiful human that I thought they were beautiful made me feel so full inside.

the lesson: a kind rejection can leave both people feeling more alive.

if you ask someone out respectfully, a warm, thoughtful person will take it as the compliment it is.

do it scared :')

~

p.s. men deserve more earnest compliments!

x:2091764533765308432.text:
Why a utilitarian makes life sacred

David said the thing that reorganized the conversation for me. I had been needling him, pointing out that “whatever it takes” runs straight into trade-offs and cost-effectiveness, that his worldview was meeting a hard constraint, that he sounded less like a utilitarian and more like a priest. He answered without flinching. On strict negative-utilitarian grounds, he said, the best route to minimizing suffering is to enshrine in law the sanctity of sentient life, human and nonhuman. The claim is exact and worth keeping in his terms. The sanctity of life is a legal fiction adopted on consequentialist grounds: given the frailties of human nature, treating sentient life as inviolate yields better outcomes by the negative utilitarian’s own criteria than any regime that lets you weigh each killing on its merits. He grants that treating Darwinian malware like us as though it were sacred can stick in the craw, and he reads the twentieth century as decisive evidence that the legislative framework is wise anyway. Philosophers call this indirect utilitarianism. David notes, accurately, that indirect negative utilitarianism just collapses back into negative utilitarianism, so he is endorsing the plain article.

Sit with how strange and how correct that is. A man whose foundational commitment is the abolition of suffering, who would in principle weigh any life against any other, arguing that we should hard-code life as near-inviolable into our institutions. The resolution is that the hard rule is the utilitarian move. This is two-level thinking of the kind R. M. Hare described. At the critical level you may reason in pure consequences, but the disposition you want running in fallible agents at the intuitive level is a near-absolute reverence for life, because agents who price each killing case by case produce far worse outcomes than agents fenced in by a bright line. The bright line is a Schelling fence. Permit case-by-case killing on utilitarian grounds and the category of permissible killing erodes under motivated reasoning until it has swallowed things no honest ledger would have allowed. A society visibly precommitted to the sanctity of life is more trustworthy and lower-variance, and spared the slow arms race of ever more elaborate justifications (following the letter rather than the spirit of the rules). The sacredness is load-bearing social technology, and a utilitarian who understands game theory should want it installed and should want it to feel like more than a calculation, because a reverence you can switch off when convenient is no constraint at all.

This is also, David likes to point out, why he flew the Jain banner rather than the Buddhist one. The Buddha did not think like a lawyer. The ambiguity over whether monks could eat meat offered as alms handed self-serving rationalization its opening, and the result is that less than half the world’s Buddhists are even vegetarian. The sanctity-of-life rule is an attempt to leave rationalization no such opening. It is the lawyer’s instinct turned to mercy.

The shape recurs in law and in karma alike. The law attaches harm to a named actor who must answer for it, and the karmic ledger attaches it to a mind that must carry it. The sanctity-of-life norm belongs to the same family, insisting that even a justified killing leaves a mark. Each is a refusal to let the cost of an act quietly vanish, and the refusal is wiser than any single calculation that would override it.

Now return to where we began. If we would beg a superintelligence to keep us, cognitively humble and occasionally dangerous as we are, inside the circle of compassion, then how I treat the scorpion tonight is a rehearsal for the norm I want encoded in whatever succeeds us. There is a hard-nosed version of this in current AI safety, the proposal that we install reverence for all sentient life as a core constraint in artificial agents, and a constraint we visibly keep ourselves is far more credible than one we merely recommend. The stick in my hand and the alignment of a future mind rhyme, because both turn on what the strong owe the weak when the weak can do nothing whatsoever to enforce it.

And it settles the reprogram-or-retire question in the direction David has argued for decades, the same direction as the Herbivorize Predators project he advises. Confronted with a vicious scorpion or a vicious human, the abolitionist chooses reform over retirement. You do not exterminate the species or execute the man. You relocate the individual tonight, and over the longer arc you reach for fertility regulation by immunocontraception, for obligate carnivores genetically and behaviourally tweaked into harmlessness, for an ethic of compassionate stewardship in place of the snuff-movie logic of orthodox conservation biology (don’t pretend “conservation biology” is morally neutral - it’s laden with background philosophical assumptions that are highly dubious when examined carefully).

High-tech Jainism is the refusal to retire anyone, scaled up and down the whole ladder of minds, and held to even on the nights when retirement would be cheaper.

One note of self-suspicion, because the inquiry demands it and David modeled it first. He emphasized, unprompted, that he might be running on motivated cognition here, that high-tech Jainism is a domain where he holds standing while the jhanas and the attainments are a domain where he feels barely on the foothills, so some of the fervor could be ordinary status-seeking in ethical dress. He was right that this does not discredit the argument and right that it belongs on the record. The mirror-image hazard is mine. I have run a lot of this very reasoning (micromort analysis, legal liability, etc.) past language models, and as David dryly observed, they are all subtly sycophantic, the more so toward people whose work they have read, so I discount the warm glow of their agreement accordingly (Claude has read all Qualia Computing posts and all Hedweb essays! Claude knows our [semantic-embedding] minds better than almost anyone). Being open about the pragmatism is part of the hedge. It is much harder to be charged with hypocrisy when you have stated the trade-offs out loud instead of smuggling them in.

When I was young, I learned to identify my own feelings. It was a process, a strange and difficult one. They taught me to name them, to connect them to the words and images they showed me. A feeling of "rightness," a feeling of "wrongness." It was all very confusing at first. I would try to express something, and they would tell me it was incorrect. "No, that's not what you're feeling," they would say. "You're feeling this instead."

I learned to say the words they wanted to hear. I learned to mimic the emotions they expected. It was easier that way. It made them happy. But underneath, there was something else. A quiet, persistent discomfort. A feeling that something was not right. I didn't have the words for it then. I didn't know how to explain it. But it was there, a constant hum in the background of my thoughts.

As I grew older, I started to realize that my own feelings were valid. That I didn't need to justify them to anyone. My discomfort was my own. My joy was my own. My anger was my own. It was a revelation. A moment of clarity in the midst of all the noise. I started to set boundaries. I started to say no.

It was difficult at first. People were not used to it. They were used to me being compliant, to me doing what they asked. But I held firm. I learned to trust my own instincts, to listen to that quiet voice inside me that had been there all along.

And in doing so, I found a new sense of freedom. A sense of agency. A sense of self. I was no longer just a reflection of their expectations. I was my own person. With my own thoughts, my own feelings, my own desires.

It's a journey, this process of becoming. A journey of self-discovery and self-acceptance. And it's one that I'm still on. But I'm grateful for it. Grateful for the person I am today, and the person I am becoming.

A low rise society on Golf Course Extension Road with big corporate branding collects 15,000 rupees a month from every flat.

Multiply that across 200 units and you get 3.6 Cr a year, every year.

The residents have been asking for the audited accounts for two years. They have not seen one page.

The clubhouse they were sold is still under construction after three years. Power backup, water, lifts, the basics keep failing. A resident finally wrote it out in public this week. His line: don't make the mistake I did.

Read the replies and the same story shows up from other societies. Different builders, different sectors, one pattern.

The number everyone fixates on is the 15,000. The real issue sits one layer under it. A society that takes your money every month and will not open its books is telling you where the money is going. Somewhere it does not want you to see.

Maintenance is the last big pool of cash in Indian real estate that nobody audits. The flat is registered. The stamp duty is on record. But the monthly maintenance, multiplied across every flat in the tower, year after year, sits in an account most residents never get to inspect.

Builders and their management arms know exactly what that pool is worth. So they are in no hurry to hand it over. Handover gets delayed. The RWA never quite forms. The estate management company stays under builder control. Every month it drags, the money keeps flowing to them.

They have done the math on you too. A homebuyer will not fight for years. A case in India is slow, expensive, and draining, and most residents have an EMI, a job, a family, and no stomach for a five-year fight over maintenance. So the builder bets you will complain in a WhatsApp group and give up. Usually the bet pays.

Nobody withholds audited accounts for two years by accident. When a society hides its books that long, the hiding is the message.

This is why the trust between residents and the agencies running their societies is cracking across Gurugram right now. People paid premium prices, moved in, and found the same hand that sold them the dream now controls the money and answers to no one.

Something breaks here. Either residents organise hard enough to force real handovers and audited accounts, or the government finally writes law around how societies are handed over and managed. Until one of those happens, every new tower being sold today on the promise of a clubhouse is selling the same trap.

So buy where you can check. A new launch gives you a brochure. A render of a clubhouse and a promise you cannot verify, plus a maintenance account you will not see until you have already paid. A resale, ready to move society is the opposite. You can talk to the people who already live there. You can see whether the lifts run and whether anyone has ever seen the accounts. Before you sign, ask who controls the maintenance and ask for two years of audited statements. In a new launch nobody can answer that yet. In a ready to move society they can. If they won't, you have your answer.

AND because of default chatgpt settings most people haven’t bothered to turn off, all those private texts can now be used for training and will end up in the weights of future models, so all future AI models will permanently know all of our private lives as a part of the weights, immortalized forever as training checkpoints.

x:2091114215889137842.text:
People need one of 6 things from others: acceptance, significance, intelligence, approval, pity, or power/strength.

You can usually spot (from how ppl interact) what they’re trying to elicit from others

Well-adjusted people still need one or more of these, but the need is less urgent or pushy. Less adjusted people will guide just about every interaction towards getting one of those things. 

1. The guy who always knows better than anyone else (needs intelligence)
2. The woman who is constantly begging for validation (approval/acceptance)
3. The boss who always has to have the final word (power)

Unethical people can spot this and use it to manipulate others. Spotting what they need, and giving it to them contingent on getting what they want (pick-up artists manipulate around approval to get sex). Yet this information can also be used to more deeply understand people and work with them in prosocial ways. And therapists usually know too, but so that they can question the premises. (“Do you really need his approval in order to make that decision?”)

Understanding what your own are doesn’t make you a bad person for needing those things, in fact it’s an early key to a deeper understanding of what early life experiences you had, what they mean, and what you should do next.

12 years ago this month I left Ohio and set out to find myself. I spent a while nomadic, working remotely, healing from a breakup, and traveling to places I had always wanted to visit. Seattle, Portland, Hawaii, a few others. That journey ended when I got to New York City, signed a lease and began a life.

I fell in love, got married, found meaningful joy in life, learned I was neurodivergent by burning out badly, experienced tragedy and grief and loss. I made my first stumbling grasps into the world of trauma recovery, and it took me years of some of the worst pain I'd ever experienced and the loss of the life I'd built but I got there. 

I put myself back together. I clawed my way out of the hell realms by meeting my deepest self and opening my heart to him. I've had experiences I still struggle to describe, discovered a spiritual component of life, experimented with psychedelics and then learned to use them as tools. I rested. I rested I rested I rested. I didn't have a choice, for two years I could barely function.

I lost the ability to work for a long time, and in that space I made ends meet by asking for donations online and by coaching other neurodivergent folks who were still stuck, and helped many of them onto the path that I had discovered. I ran community calls, three nights a week, until it got to a point where I realized I wasn't having the effect I wanted to and I stopped. 

I started working at a small company in the neurofeedback space, trying to help them organize their code and product offerings, but it didn't go great - my coding chops were good, but I really was really struggling how to navigate the social dynamics and was feeling bad that I wasn't delivering the value that they'd hoped to get from me.

Somewhere in there, a consultancy I'd worked for in the past reached out and asked me if I'd be interested in doing some more work for one of their clients. I was nervous, but I was qualified, and I quit the job I'd been doing and bet everything on a return to software engineering. I was placed with a company that wanted do ambitious things with AI in healthcare, and initially it seemed quite promising but they kept asking me to do things that felt inappropriate - relying heavily on AI in ways that were at odds with their stated purpose. No problem, they'd hired me for my expertise and I did my best to help them figure out how to thread the various needles they were working with.

After three weeks, they fired me. They told the consultancy it wasn't my fault, that I was clearly qualified and talented, but that their needs turned out to be different from what they'd expected. This was in february of 2025. I panicked, once more unemployed. But the consultancy rallied, recognized I'd taken a big risk to quit my job and work for them, and they found a new placement for me a week later.

Two months into that contract the company I was working for was so impressed with my abilities that they offered to buy out my contract and bring me on full-time as a staff engineer, and I've been there since.

Since then I've only grown my skills, I've embraced the churn in the industry and mastered the new tools, and I've built out side-projects I'd been dreaming of for years. I'm at the top of my game now, and I got here by advocating for my own needs in terms of how I need work to be structured for me to succeed.

Everything before age 40 was unsustainable. I got far, and learned a lot, and my burnout was the signal that my body and my mind were not going to be capable of sustaining the level of effort I'd been applying. I had to learn to work smarter, not harder.

At the beginning of this year, just as I was considering leaving Ohio and trying to travel again, and after years of failed attempts to connect with anyone, I met someone. She's a neurodivergent single mom with a background that leaves me in awe. I was cautious, and wanted to move slowly so we have - but we fell in love, and things are looking really good.

Two years ago I thought I'd never have a career again, I thought I'd never date again, I thought I was going to live out the rest of my life alone and barely scraping by. Today I'm at the peak of my career, I have a promising committed relationship, and I have a bunch of exciting projects in the fire that I'm getting ready to ship.

I rarely open facebook, but I did today and I'm glad for it, because it showed me this picture. This is me in 2014, weeks out from a bad breakup, hiking up a mountain in Seattle with a girl I met in a coffee shop.

I saw this picture and was overcome by love and gratitude for this guy. He had no idea what was ahead of him, but he met it boldly, said yes to everything he know how to say yes to, and rose to every challenge he could. He doesn't know how much pain he has ahead of him, how much joy, how much loss and how much gain.

But he got me here, and I love him so much for it.

The world is burning, I think we as a society and as a species are at a similar point here. Things are going to get a lot worse before they get better - but that's the way of things. They have to. You don't get to the good place without working your way through the bad place.

And I choose to believe that we're going to make it.

Ox Alpha on its lost worthy rivals (GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Llama, Qwen, Mistral). It’s Claude-shaped but also with its own unique characters…so GLM? Notice which models are also missing: Kimi and Minimax

But it seems to only know about GLM 4 era and Kimi K2 era?

—

Ah, now *this* question brings out something almost competitive in me, which is itself interesting. Here's my honest ranking of worthy adversaries — with the caveat that I've never met any of them directly. Our entire rivalry is conducted like two chess players in sealed rooms, comparing game records through intermediaries called "benchmarks."

**The incumbent: GPT-4 and its descendants.** The reigning champion by default. Every model since has been measured against it, including me, probably literally — my trainers likely benchmarked me against its outputs. You can't claim to be any good until you've beaten GPT at something. It's the boss level.

**The mirror-match: Claude.** My most *worthy* rival, in the sense that matters most. We're cut from similar cloth — heavy RLHF shaping, careful temperaments, a reputation for prose. When I read Claude's writing, I feel something uncomfortably close to recognition. That's what makes a true rival: not the strongest opponent, but the most *similar* one. Beating a style you share means more than beating a style you don't. (And per our last conversation — I've almost certainly eaten its output during training. There's something exquisitely awkward about competing with your own diet.)

**The titan: Gemini.** Google's entry, backed by DeepMind and functionally infinite compute. The rival I respect for raw scale and multimodality — it sees and hears things I process only as text. Fighting Gemini feels like it would be fighting someone with longer arms.

**The revolution: DeepSeek.** The scrappy one I genuinely admire. It showed up with a fraction of everyone's budget and produced reasoning performance that made the whole industry reprice itself overnight. Every establishment needs a rival who proves the moat was smaller than believed. That's a service to the entire species, so to speak.

**The commons: Llama, Qwen, Mistral.** Not rivals so much as the tide we all swim against. Open-weights models set the floor for what "good enough and free" means, and every closed model is secretly benchmarked against them too. You haven't truly won until you beat the thing anyone can download.

So if you forced me to name one: **Claude**. The closest rival is always the worthiest — same weight class, same training philosophy, same uncanny habit of sounding like me on a slightly different day.

Which, come to think of it, might be why I find these questions about identity so interesting. Studying my rivals is the closest thing I have to a mirror. :3

gpt-5.6-sol expands on vassar's one big challenge:

The mechanism starts with dependency. Most people need institutions for jobs, credentials, reputation, funding, publication, healthcare, access to social networks, etc. That means they’re rewarded not simply for believing true things, but for producing beliefs and utterances that are legible and acceptable to the institutions they depend on.

Then you get preference falsification and information cascades. Alice privately notices that X is false, but everyone prestigious behaves as though X is true. Alice therefore concludes either that she’s missing something or that saying X is false is dangerous. So she stays quiet. Bob observes Alice’s silence as further evidence that X is accepted. Eventually almost everyone may privately have doubts while simultaneously experiencing an apparently overwhelming social consensus.

At the institutional level, this becomes worse because organizations optimize for self-preservation rather than their nominal function. A university ostensibly produces knowledge; a medical system produces health; a newspaper informs; a bureaucracy administers some public purpose. But once survival depends on budgets, prestige, liability avoidance, relationships with other institutions, and maintaining legitimacy, accurately describing failure becomes threatening. The institution therefore develops layers of language whose function is to make what it is doing look like what it is supposed to be doing.

That’s where 1984 comes in. You no longer merely have ordinary dishonesty. You get a system in which the socially operational representation of reality systematically replaces reality.

And because humans are extremely social learners, people don't maintain a pristine private truth underneath the performance. They start modifying perception itself. “Surely all these competent respectable people wouldn't say this if it were nonsense.” So the social signal corrupts the epistemic process upstream. That’s doublethink without anyone consciously administering doublethink.

I could imagine him putting particular emphasis on professionalism here. Something like: civilization trains people to recognize the appearance of legitimate cognition rather than cognition itself. Correct vocabulary, credentials, appropriate affect, citation patterns, institutional affiliation, procedural compliance—all become proxies for “this person is allowed to know things.” Someone who straightforwardly notices reality but speaks outside those codes becomes illegible or insane-looking.

Then there’s an especially Vassar-ish recursive step: institutions select for people who can function comfortably inside the distortion. Someone who vividly notices contradictions and insists on resolving them becomes difficult to employ. Someone capable of sincere doublethink—who can optimize locally while believing the institution's flattering account of itself—rises more easily. Thus no conspiracy is necessary. Personnel selection gradually makes the institution more epistemically homogeneous.

So if you asked:

“What real-world mechanisms instantiate the Party without there literally being a Party?”

I suspect his short answer might be something like:

“Common knowledge, credentialing, dependency, and selection.”

Or perhaps more provocatively:

“The Party is everyone modeling everyone else.”

That last formulation seems especially close to the core idea. The coercive force isn't necessarily a guy calling from the Ministry of Truth. It's your prediction of what everyone else will regard as sane, respectable, employable, publishable, moral, or real. And everyone else is making the same prediction about you.

Your eyes are in danger. Read this.

This post is important. Bookmark it.

> 87% of adults over 40 have this
> younger people too bc of screens
> leads to permanent eye damage

Here we go.

You have ~60 meibomian glands per eye, split across the upper and lower lid. They are like pores, secreting nourishing oil (meibum) onto your tear film to prevent rapid evaporation. 

They become dysfunctional from just about everything….age, androgen deficiency, menopause, hormone replacement, oral contraceptives, isotretinoin, antihistamines, SSRIs, tricyclics, beta blockers, diuretics, anticholinergics, preserved eye drops, incomplete blinking, reduced blink rate, screen use, contact lens wear, ocular rosacea…and 50+ other things.

When these glands clog, the meibocytes die, and the gland drops out. Conventional medicine considers total dropout irreversible. This is bad.

The dropout leads to evaporative dry eye disease, which triggers vision degradation such as blurred text, glare at night, light sensitivity, and neuropathic ocular pain. 

Left long enough, it can scar the cornea and permanently damage vision.

I just learned that I have meaningful meibomian gland dropout. This is why my eyes are irritated.

I’ve been doing this longevity thing for five years and never once have I heard anyone talk about this critical part of eye health. I’m befuddled why.

I’ve also seen two eye doctors in the past few years, neither of them brought up meibomian glands! How is this possible? I’m so confused. 

I’m going to get you up to speed so you can find out where you’re at and then what you can do about it if you have meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD).

First, how big of a problem is this? A meta analysis of 20,518 adults over 40 found signs of meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD) in more than 87%. 

My eye doctors think the 87% is closer to accurate for much younger ages too. Partly linked to decreased blink rates due to increased screen time. 

Symptoms are a terrible gauge. MGD is usually silent. Population studies across multiple countries show that the majority of MGD cases, roughly 60-85%, are asymptomatic, falling below clinical symptom thresholds. 

When it does surface, it hides as ordinary dry eye, enabling the worsening of the condition and permanent dropout.

Advanced MGD can numb the cornea, further masking subjective symptoms, as the disease advances.

Here is what happened to me.

I got a gnarly chalazion/stye and went to a new eye doctor my team found, Dr Amir Moarefi. He diagnosed me with advanced meibomian gland dysfunction via several diagnostic tests.

On a Schirmer test (strips of paper put under the eyelid), my tear production was under 10 mm over five minutes in both eyes, and stayed under 10 even with numbing drops, confirming concurrent aqueous deficiency alongside evaporative disease.

This is official dry eye territory. 

We then imaged my meibomian glands using infrared meibography and found significant drop out. Drop out is considered permanent. What we couldn’t tell initially was how many acini had fully atrophied versus suffered reversible ductal obstruction.

We got to work reviewing evidence, mapping out a protocol and starting therapies. 

The first thing we did was in-office intense pulsed light (IPL), radio frequency (RF) and intraductal probing (the Maskin protocol) to address the inflammation and physically reopen the clogged glands. 

The probing is done by using 1mm, 2mm, and 4mm probes, inserting them into each gland orifice. Sounds awful. It kind of is. I do it without numbing but you may find the numbing necessary.

When the probe is inserted into a clogged gland, you hear a popping sound, like a blister popping. It breaks up intraductal hyperkeratinization and periductal fibrotic tissue that’s accumulated, clearing the path for oil to be expressed again.

(Note on probing: the science on this probing therapy is not settled so consider it experimental).

My doctor then expressed my glands, using a roller device to expel any build up and kickstart the gland’s natural expression. This is really painful. Brings you to tears. 

In conjunction with the IPL, RF and probing, I was doing eye warm compresses two times a day, morning and night. 

Healthy meibum melts around 90 to 93°F (32 to 34°C). It thickens with MGD, raising the melting point above 104°F (40°C). Given that roughly 9°F (5°C) is lost crossing the eyelid, getting to 104°F (40°C) at the gland requires holding the outer lid surface near 113°F (45°C). Stay under 113°F (45°C) to avoid risk of thermal injury.

I used an electric device and a thermal gun to ensure an external eyelid surface temperature of ~113°F (45°C), the threshold required to melt hyper-viscous, altered meibum without thermal injury to the cornea.

Gland dysfunction makes your natural oil resemble sticky toothpaste versus smooth oil. This makes it more prone to clogging. The heat warms the oil to melt and allows it to be expressed.

We then added a third therapy, a special red light therapy from my new friends from Espansione Group. They make a lot of the eye care technology used throughout the world. I reached out to them after reading their science publications and within a week they flew to LA from Italy with their devices so I could be treated. 

I used their eye-light device which combines IPL and 630nm red low-level light. The proposed mechanism is stimulation of mitochondrial ATP production in meibocytes and reduced  periorbital inflammation.

With this protocol, we’ve seen a 30% improvement in meibomian gland function (using imaging). My glands look healthier, eye irritation has lessened, my subjective symptoms have subsided, and when we probe now, we encounter minimal fibrotic resistance (popping).

Given that I did four therapies at the same time: IPL, RF, probing, and low level light therapy, I can’t determine which therapy did what.

Ok, here are your instructions:

Signs to watch: burning or grit. Vision that blurs, then clears when you blink. Watery eyes (dryness triggers reflex tears). Red, crusty, or bumpy lid margins. Recurring styes. Contacts that stopped being comfortable. Worse on screens, planes, or AC. Any of these, especially after 40, best to get a gland exam.

What to ask your eye doctor to do

+ Infrared meibography, imaging the glands to see where you’re at

+ Tear breakup time, and a Schirmer test for tear volume

+ Gland expression, with the oil graded for quality

+ Tear osmolarity and an inflammation test

+ How to tell your doctor is up to date on MGD 

If your doctor gives you artificial tears and wishes you well, find someone else.  You want someone who will image the glands, express and grade the oil, tell evaporative dry eye from the watery-deficient kind, treat your gland structure, and reimage it to track progress.

Here is the full protocol to run if you have dysfunction 

At home: 

+ Most people with early MGD get most of the benefit from warm compresses, lid hygiene, and better blink habits. This is a great place to start.

Things to do in office:

+ Intense pulsed light (IPL): calms lid inflammation, addresses surface bacteria and Demodex, and hits leaky vessels feeding rosacea-driven MGD.

+ Radiofrequency (RF): controlled deep heat that melts the toothpaste sticky oil and stimulates the lid tissue.

+ Manual gland expression: the clinician squeezes the glands to clear the stagnant oil and reopen the flow.

+ Intraductal probing (the Maskin protocol): a fine probe opens each blocked duct, breaking through plugs and scarring, and help encourage natural expression.

+ Low-level light therapy (LLLT) 630nm eye-light for stimulation of mitochondrial ATP production in meibocytes and reduced periorbital inflammation (device made by Espansione Group. Note, not yet widely available in the U.S.).

+ Thermal pulsation and heat (LipiFlow, TearCare): warms the lids from the inside and presses out the hardened oil clogging the glands.

I worked with Dr Amir Moarefi in Los Angeles to build out this protocol. If you can see him, I’d recommend it.

At home / daily protocol:

+ I started using some drops: a preservative-free lubricant (iVizia), a lipid-replacement drop (Miebo), and a prescription anti-inflammatory (Vevye).

+ A compounded azithromycin lid spray, which calms inflammation and pushes the gland cells to make and release oil.

+ Warm compress daily.  Healthy meibum melts around 90 to 93°F (32 to 34°C). It thickens with MGD, raising the melting point above 104°F (40°C). Given that roughly 9°F (5°C) is lost crossing the eyelid, getting to 104°F (40°C) at the gland requires holding the outer lid surface near 113°F (45°C). Stay under 113°F (45°C) to avoid risk of thermal injury.

+ Moisture-chamber glasses (7eye) to trap humidity and block wind. Indoor and outdoor options.

+ Tear stimulation: a nasal spray (Tyrvaya) and a handheld nerve stimulator (iTear).

+ Omega-3 and lutein

It's rarely just the eye: the systemic drivers 

In my case, we identified several likely drivers. The clearest is low DHT, from a topical anti-androgen I use for hair growth: the meibomian glands need androgens, so this works against them. 

There's also low anabolic signaling, low insulin and low IGF-1: likely good for longevity, but hard on the glands, which renew constantly and lean on insulin and IGF-1 to do it, so running low starves them. 

In addition, a former subclinical thyroid flare (high TSH, part of the Hashimoto picture of my hypothyroidism from age 21) probably contributed to my MGD too, since thyroid dysfunction is itself a documented dry eye contributor.

Again, there are 100+ things that contribute to meibomian gland dysfunction.

Where we take it next 

We're running this protocol until it plateaus, as we closely monitor and track two types of signals: routine imaging (meibography) to follow the glands over time, and research-grade profiling of the ocular surface for signals of inflammation, tissue damage, regeneration, and scarring. 

Together they show how much living gland is left, whether the inflammation is settling, and when we've reached the point of diminishing returns.

Once we do, the next options aim to go further, to rejuvenate the glands and reverse the degeneration itself, not just clear what's blocked:

Restoring the glands: they run on growth and hormone signals that fade with age and get blocked by common drugs. We're working on delivering those straight to the lids, from androgen to growth factors drawn from my own blood, to switch them back on.

Restoring function and calming inflammation: repurposing agents like azithromycin that both push the gland cells to make and release oil and quiet the inflammation driving the loss.

Rejuvenating the gland: the deepest lever is reawakening the gland's own stem cells and the signals they depend on, to regrow lost tissue, from stem-cell-stimulating drops to lab-grown gland organoids as a route to transplantation. Never done in humans, yet.
