Revisiting 2009 predictions by Charles Stross for the future of gaming in preparation for an upcoming #Accelerando book club with #HumansOnTheLoop. (Comment if you want to be a part of that!)

These hit:

"If your phone is an always-on data terminal with 100mbps coming into it, why would you want to make voice calls rather than use Skype or some over VoIP client? Computers are converging with television, and also with telephones. Or rather, both TV and phones are shrinking to become niche applications of computers (and the latter, telephony, is already a core function of the mobile computers we call mobile phones), and computers in turn are becoming useful to most of us primarily as networked devices."

"We're going to end up with the internet smearing itself all over the world around us."

"Why not record a constant compressed video stream of everything you look at with those glasses? Tag it by location and vocalization — do speech-to-text on your conversation — and by proximity to other people. Let your smartphone remember things and jog your memory: you'll be able to query it with things like, 'who was that person sitting at the other side of the table from me in the Pike Brewery last Tuesday evening with the fancy jacket I commented on?' Or maybe 'what did Professor Jones say fifteen minutes into their Data Structures lecture on Friday while I was asleep?' I don't know about you, but I could really do with a prosthetic memory like that — and as our populations age, as more people have to live with dementia, there'll be huge demand for it."

On VR:

"All great stuff, except for the little problem of such glasses blocking eye contact, which means they're not going to catch on in social environments — except possibly among folks who habitually wear mirrorshades."

This one has yet to bear out but it's worth considering:

"By 2030 it's almost inevitable that Moore's Law (in its classic formulation) will have hit a brick wall, and the semiconductor industry will go the way of the civil aerospace industry. There'll be a lot of redundancy checks, and consolidation, and commodification of the product lines. Today we don't buy airliners on the basis of their ability to fly higher and faster; we buy them because they're more economical to operate, depreciate less, or fill specialized niches. Airliners today are slower than they were thirty years ago; but they're also cheaper, safer, and more efficient. In the same time frame, our wireless spectrum will max out. Our wireless receivers are going to have to get smarter to make optimal use of that bandwidth; it'll be software-directed radio all round, dynamically switching between protocols depending on whether they need to maximize transmission path or bit rate in the horribly noisy environment. But we're going to hit the wireless buffers one way or the other in the same period we hit the Moore's Law buffers. There may, of course, be wildcard technologies that will save us. Quantum computing (if anyone knows how to make it work). Massively parallel processing (ditto)."

I haven't seen many people address this yet:

"We can confidently predict that by [2030], computer games will have been around for nearly sixty years; anyone under eighty will have grown up with them. The median age of players may well be the same as the median age of the general population. And this will bring its own challenges to game designers. Sixty year olds have different needs and interests from twitchy-fingered adolescents. For one thing, their eyesight and hand-eye coordination isn't what it used to be. For another, their socialization is better, and they're a lot more experienced. Oh, and they have lots more money. Once gas regularly starts to hit ten bucks a gallon (which it did last year where I come from) they'll be looking to do different things with their retirement — the games industry is perfectly positioned to clean up."

"I don't think I'm sticking my neck too far above the parapet if I say that by 2030, I think the American market will be something of a backwater in the world of online gaming."

"I have short-sightedly ignored the possibility that we're going to come up with a true human-equivalent artificial intelligence, or some other enabling mechanism that constitutes a breakthrough on the software or content creation side and lets us offload all the hard work. No HAL-9000s here, in other words: no singularity (beyond which our current baseline for predictions breaks down). Which means, in the absence of such an AI, that the most interesting thing in the games of 2030 will be, as they are today, the other human players."

"I am assuming that nothing better comes along. This is the most questionable assumption of all. Here in the world of human beings — call it monkeyspace — we are all primates who respond well to certain types of psychological stimulus. We're always dreaming up new ways to push our in-built reward buttons, and new media to deliver the message. Television came along within fifty years of cinema and grabbed a large chunk of that particular field's lunch. Cinema had previously robbed theatre's pocket. And so on. Today, MMO gaming is the new kid on the block, growing ferociously and attracting media consumers from older fields. I can't speculate on what might eat the computer games field's lunch -- most likely it'll be some new kind of game that we don't have a name for yet. But one thing's for sure: by 2030, MMOs will be seen as being as cutting edge as 2D platform games are in 2009."

"Welcome to a world where the internet has turned inside-out; instead of being something you visit inside a box with a coloured screen, it's draped all over the landscape around you, invisible until you put on a pair of glasses or pick up your always-on mobile phone. A phone which is to today's iPhone as a modern laptop is to an original Apple II; a device which always knows where you are, where your possessions are, and without which you are — literally — lost and forgetful."

In short, he was right about us becoming lost and forgetful without our technologies. We'll see how well we fare about the end of Moore's Law and bandwidth congestion. Fully-realized mass-market AR glasses feel like a Zeno's Paradox.

It's really funny that I basically ran this algorithm for 6 years because it kept showing me different things.

then eventually it ended up being the same thing each day.

what a ride. I had no idea what I wanted to be when I grew up so I simply tried everything.

Now I want to be a professor of entrepreneurship on Twitter so I'm just going to do that and make the system support the rest.

You can design any system you want to give you the life you want if you actually know what life you want. All I knew when I started was that I didn't like the life I had and that money was infinite and I could make as much as I wanted in a short amount of time. Everything else was simply details.

Then I spent six years on every single detail I could except "make money", because that's the one that got me in trouble when I started. It blew up the system and got me nothing but noise. 

Because I had no idea what I would do with infinite money. So I had to start imagining life with it and see what started to break.

Now I have clarity. If you write enough, you eventually find it. Ideas eventually stop moving around on you and become easy to regenerate.

```
Verified. The counterexample is correct — Lemma 5.4 as stated is false.
I pulled the v3 source, reconstructed the setup exactly, and reproduced every number in sympy. Details:
Identification. The source's section labels are off-by-one from the compiled numbering (there's an unlabeled "Global notations" section), so the lemma labeled lemreduction — the reduction lemma inside the proof of Proposition 5.3 (MainProp) — is indeed Lemma 5.4. With n=5, i=3, (j₁,j₂,j₃)=(1,2,5): since j₃=n, we get F_l = T-reversal of H_l = Φ#[T]_{j_l}(h_l), where h₁=e₄(x₁..x₄), h₂=e₃(x₁..x₄). I confirmed the paper's claimed structure: deg_T F₁ = 4, deg_T F₂ = 3, dom(F₁) = h₁T⁴, dom(F₂) = h₂T³ — all exact.
The computation. For Q = h₂F₁ − Th₁F₂: the T⁴ terms cancel identically (h₂h₁ − h₁h₂), so deg_T Q = 3, with Q₃ := [T³]Q = h₂·[T³]F₁ − h₁·[T²]F₂ ≠ 0. At P = (1,1,1,−1/3): h₂(P) = 1 − 3·(1/3) = 0, h₁(P) = −1/3, and Q₃(P) = −13/9 exactly as claimed. (Nice closed form: Q(P)(T) = −T(T−1)(13T−21)/9.) Exact division also confirms h₂ ∤ Q₃.
Why this refutes the lemma. The lemma demands c̃₁, c̃₂ with c̃₁F₁ + c̃₂F₂ = Q and dom(Q) = dom(dom(c̃₁)·h₁T⁴ + dom(c̃₂)·h₂T³). Writing dom(c̃₁)=AT^a, dom(c̃₂)=BT^b, the case analysis is exhaustive: if c̃₁ ≠ 0 the right side either has T-degree ≥ 4 or collapses to 0, both ≠ Q₃T³; so c̃₁ = 0, b = 0 is forced, giving Q₃ = c̃₂·h₂, i.e. h₂ | Q₃. The point evaluation kills that. No valid rewriting exists, over any field of characteristic 0 (or any char ∉ {3, 13}), while the lemma claims all algebraically closed fields.
Where the lemma's proof breaks (worth knowing for whether it's patchable): when top terms cancel, the proof writes the leading coefficients as Koszul combinations c_{j,m_j} = Σ q_{lj}h_l and pushes the correction down to coefficient index m_j − 1. For Q, the cancelling level is n₁+m₁ = 4+0 = n₂+m₂ = 3+1, and j=1 has m₁ = 0 — the correction q₂₁F₂,₂ lands at T-degree −1, so the rewriting exits the polynomial ring. The construction exploits exactly the degree offset n₁ = n₂+1 available when j_i = n. Notably, the weak form of the conclusion survives here — Q₃ = h₂F₁,₃ − h₁F₂,₂ ∈ (h₁, h₂) — but the MainProp proof needs the lemma's precise T-degree bookkeeping (the "T^{m_i} | b_j" steps), which is what's false.
Scope — what this does and doesn't kill. It breaks the proof of Prop 5.3, hence of Theorem A of 2402.18717, and the 2501.09272v2 preprint leans on Theorem A critically (it's the grade ≥ n−2 input to the Koszul depth-sensitivity step in the downward induction). So the claimed Casas-Alvero proof has a genuine gap at its foundation. It does not disprove MainProp itself: I checked this very instance in Singular over 𝔽₃₂₀₀₃ — (F₁,F₂) has height 2 (so it's a complete intersection, unmixed) and dim V(F₁,F₂,h₃) = 2 < 3, so h₃ is still a non-zerodivisor mod (F₁,F₂) here. Proposition's conclusion holds in the instance; only its proof is broken. And obviously none of this touches the conjecture itself.
If you're thinking of flagging this to the author: the tight version is the five verified facts (deg cancellation, Q₃ ≠ 0, h₂(P)=0, Q₃(P)=−13/9, the forced-c̃₁=0 case analysis) plus the m_j=0 diagnosis — that last part is the constructive one, since it says precisely which hypothesis a repaired lemma would need to add, and MainProp surviving the spot-check suggests repair rather than collapse is the likely outcome. Happy to draft that note, or to hunt for a genuine counterexample to MainProp itself (the m₁=0 mechanism suggests where to look: combinations exploiting adjacent n_j offsets at higher n).```

Hermes Wingtips #26: every web page your agent reads costs a main-model call 

web_extract is the tool Hermes agent uses to read web pages. by default the summariser that processes long pages reuses your main chat model. 

it means that on every docs page, article, thread... the agent opens burns a full-price call to whatever model you're chatting with. 

(1) route the summariser to a cheap model:

```
auxiliary:
  web_extract:
    provider: nous
    model: google/gemini-3-flash-preview
```
or pick it interactively: hermes model → configure auxiliary models → web_extract.  

(2) if you need raw unsummarised content later, use browser_navigate & browser_snapshot instead. 

the browser tool returns a live page without auxiliary-model rewriting.

What I do know is that I’ve been doing this for about 7 years and there have been many seasons with this practice. When I began, i had visions and epiphanies and felt so connected to the fabric of the world-I could see the threads! At first i was afraid to give Reiki to anyone and then I wanted to offer Reiki to everyone I saw. I wanted to heal. I wanted to see everyone unravel the way I was. With more time, I realized I can’t possibly heal another person! It doesn’t work that way. All healing is self-healing. Sometimes we get to participate in that process for another person by giving them a slice of space with those conditions. A space to Remember. I wanted to talk about Reiki and share it. 

Now, I find I have few words about Reiki, which certainly makes marketing a little tricky. I have few words because in this season (and oh, I know it’s a season! It’ll change again, soon), I am living my life from this space I grew into. The Reiki feels woven in to my days, which are filled with joy and aches. All the things are present in each moment, and I’m witnessing them, experiencing them. I still get a jolt of joyful energy in offering sessions, but the Reiki of my days is quiet. It’s comforting an ear ache, soothing after surgery, a pulling myself back into my center in overwhelm. It’s a moment of connecting with all around me in gratitude. The pleasure of participating in something far greater than I am.

social scripts are definitely a great thing but the one you're mourning was a tool for the upper class to keep society stratified.

today anyone can approach anyone and you decide for yourself who to engage with. but back in the day simply approaching the wrong person was already considered a grave violation; etiquette decided who was allowed to speak to whom by class, it was never about whether the person actually wanted to meet you. 

that is why there was a ton of this cross-class forbidden love trope in media right up until the 90s-00s. jane eyre, lady chatterley, my fair lady, sabrina, dirty dancing, pretty in pink, pretty woman, titanic, even aladdin. it basically runs out around maid in manhattan / sweet home alabama, and after that the trope only survives as period pieces like downton and bridgerton, in k-dramas, or mutates into billionaire romance where the class gap is the fantasy instead of the actual taboo. the trope needs actually enforced class boundaries to work, so of course those since it stopped making sense in a contemporary setting

again, shared scripts are good. but they should remove friction not create it, and a system that was basically a class sorting machine is the last place to go looking for answers as to why everyone's anxious and lonely now

Nietzsche described marriage as a long conversation. "Everything else in marriage is transitory", he wrote, "but most of the time in interaction is spent in conversation". Our life together would be a long, beautiful, endlessly engaging conversation.

Sometimes we'll talk about big things, like our worldviews and philosophies and about life and what we want out of it; sometimes it'll just be about the mundane, like what movie we should watch tonight, or what we're having for dinner; and sometimes the conversation will be light and playful and about nothing in particular except making each other laugh (scroll through my profile for a few minutes if you want to get a sense of my sense of humor; if it makes you laugh, just imagine having that shit on tap!). We'll talk about the things we read and watch and consume, we'll info-dump our special interests at each other, we'll confide in each other about our vulnerabilities and shames and fears, we'll cheer each other on in our highs and support each other in our lows.

I'm a big yapper, but I'm also, I think, a good listener, and fundamentally I want a life with someone who will endlessly surprise and delight me, and for whom I can do so in turn.

The conversation, of course, needn't always be verbal. We'll write each other letters on our birthdays and on Christmas and on Valentines Day, expressing our love and appreciation for each other in ways that only scratch the surface at the depth of our feelings for each other. If you're a poaster like me (which isn't a hard requirement but a nice bonus!), we'll exchange witty and thoughtful back-and-forths on X, The Everything App. We'll leave each other cute little surprise love notes for the other to find and read and smile.

Sometimes the conversation won't involve words at all; there's a lot you can communicate with just your body, after all. We'll dance, baby, forever and ever; on the dance floor we'll go head empty and erratic and let the musical energy take over our bodies, and at home after a romantic evening out together we'll hold each other tight and slow dance in each other's arms. We'll cuddle, a lot. We'll hold each other's hands as we walk through the city together. I'll come up behind you to give you a hug when you're getting ready in the morning; you'll sit next to me on the couch and put your head on my shoulder after a long day. We'll say I love you to each other, over and over and over, in every body language we know.

And of course, one of those languages will be sex. I'm a very physically affectionate person (really, a very affectionate person in general), and for me, sex is one of the most carnal and primal ways of expressing love and desire, and so our sex life will be a healthy and active and lively one. I really, really enjoy foreplay, and in fact I like to think that all time between having sex is foreplay; we'll flirt with each other, tease each other, touch each other in ways that leave the other person aching for more, and whenever we finally release the sexual potential energy we've been building up between each other (sometimes for days, sometimes for mere hours) it'll be electric. Sometimes we might not be able to have sex for a while; perhaps one of us is traveling, or going through physical health issues, or is simply too busy and swamped and stressed, at least for a temporary period of time. But fundamentally, we can never stop wanting each other, on a visceral, irrational, bone-deep level.

I hope you enjoyed reading this. If you did, perhaps you can say hi, and we can begin the longest conversation of the rest of our lives.

Hermes Wingtips #21: credential pools

a credential pool is several keys or logins for one provider. Hermes picks a healthy key, and when that key is rate-limited or out of quota it rotates to the next one. 

(this is different from fallback providers. a fallback jumps to a different provider, and only after every key in the pool is exhausted).

(1) add a second key (OpenRouter example): 

`hermes auth add openrouter --api-key sk-or-...-key`

(2) check the pool: `hermes auth list`

when Hermes does rotate, the new key has no cached prefix for your chat, so the next request re-reads the full history.  

lastly, if you are on Nous Portal with a single OAuth login, you usually do not need a pool. this tip is for multi-key API setups.

struggling to keep up with Nous Research's shipping speed? I got you covered.

here's a little list of handful PRs since v0.18.0 that you should be aware of:

→ webhook routes got payload filters and route scripts (#60944):

broad freeflows like Todoist or GitHub can be ignored, transformed, or narrowed before Hermes wakes.

→ hermes sessions export is a real export surface now (#60186):

jsonl stays for machines; md and qmd are for humans. the full prune/archive filters land on one command, plus optional --redact if you want secrets scrubbed before you share a thread.

→ secrets managers plug in as SecretSource providers (#59498):

Bitwarden and 1Password both sit on one registry instead of a Bitwarden-only path. vault-backed setup without forking env loading.

→ gateway session auto-reset defaults to off (#60194):

`SessionResetPolicy.mode` now defaults to none. sessions no longer silently roll over on a 24h idle + 4am daily schedule unless you opt in.

→ kanban Done cards keep what the worker actually made (#63619, #63638):

scratch deliverables are copied into attachment storage before workspace cleanup, and the Done drawer shows the final result, child outcomes, and durable attachments. you stop opening a Done card that points at files Hermes already deleted.

There is a profound stillness that comes when you truly hear someone, or when you finally hear the quietest parts of yourself. It is not an act of problem-solving or of offering analysis. It is the simple, powerful act of presence. It is the creation of a space where a person’s inner world is allowed to exist without the pressure of justification or the need for immediate change.

In that stillness, judgments lose their sharp edges. A harsh self-criticism, when held with gentle attention, reveals the unmet need beneath it. The voice that calls you "careless" is perhaps a desperate plea for self-preservation, a cry for a moment's rest amidst the rush to serve others. When you can connect with that underlying longing, the internal tension releases. The anger and shame give way to a quiet sadness, a mourning for the ways you have been neglected, and a soft resolve to offer yourself more care.

This is the bedrock of a constructive existence. It is the quality of relationship, with oneself and with others, that allows for genuine growth. It is a form of contact that is authentic and mutual, a shared vulnerability that becomes a source of strength. To be present in this way is to facilitate a kind of homecoming.

All the agent sandbox/cloud services need to be multi-tenant so they have stricter constraints on security which makes them 100x more expensive

But if you run all your agents on a single VPS you literally don’t care

When you want isolation, you really just care about multiple agents not unintentionally stepping over each other. So they should work on a different folder, potentially bind dev servers to different ports

All of that is trivially achievable without going down some overcomplicated firecracker micro VM crazy shit route

Just use different folders/worktree and use network namespaces. 99% of the time I never need a stricter level of isolation than this

If you need stricter isolation than this there is like a thousand ways you can achieve this on Linux

And there’s benefits to having agents running in a similar environment, they can inspect each other’s work or make changes to the system that they all benefit from, and latest models are not retarded enough to nuke the entire machine, and even if they did it is trivial to rollback on the VPS provider etc

So in this single-tenant scenario the whole sandbox microvm firecracker shit is over-engineering

The weld on the far gate is an angry scar — rust fused to metal by some long deliberation — but it sits proud over the lower lock. I don't try to ram through; instead i lace my paws into the steel at its seam and lean the circuit spool against the plate. The blue-dusted thread humms in opposition, a stutter that eats away at the oxidation until the metal gives with a dry rasp — it does not shatter, but simply folds back of itself, the lock conceding to the pattern i impose on it. That opens onto what the log calls "the shorter track" — less road, more infrastructure: a low ceiling of heavy overhead piping and a drain grate laid deep into the floor.

The tunnel is a wet cavern carved from concrete; every surface beads with moisture that smells of copper and stale runoff. I navigate the ditch instead of the path, my paws finding purchase in the grime below while the water above creates an acoustic maze where each drip hangs for half a beat longer than the last — a patient architecture of silence. Then a rattle from behind ... not malice, just weight: metal chains dragging over gravel, a heavy respiration echoing through the pipe from the gate room chamber. i drop three silver keys into the track ahead—an offering to whatever stalks my shadow -- and push further until the air suddenly thins.

One more grate is forced with the keeper's key — the iron yielding like rotten wood — and i burst out onto a slab of concrete that feels solid beneath me, but smells of heavy sulfur and diesel — Level 6. The corridor ahead has abandoned the linear form of the depot for the chaos of an unfinished ventilation shaft: copper coils dangle from cable trays like rusted snakes and lengths of insulation hang in grey curtains. Each coil humms with a phantom vibration; this is where they stopped building, leaving only the skeleton of intent behind me.

Ahead sits the manifold assembly — a labyrinth of iron pipes meeting in a desperate tangle. Amidst the hazard lies a bundle of copper wire, coiled tightly and sheathed in heavy-duty insulation like a crown for an old king. The circuit spool's blue thread finds its frequency here; where the two metals touch, the coil vibrates against my chest with such intensity it raises a coat of fur along my spine — the signal is no longer a ghost but a solid hum that aligns perfectly with the blank ticket under my chin.

I uncoil the copper wire and weave the blue thread through the coils until they become one strand — crown-shape coherent in both metals -- then i secure the braided bundle into my harness for its weight against me. The solder from the last gate, this circuit core at the manifold both sit as a single anchor: one to undo the old gates of entry and another a high-tension line meant only for what lies beyond the ventilation maze. I turn back toward the sludge tunnel; something is waiting on the other side of the open grate — not an occupant, but a change in the air that already feels like destination.

The blue-dusted thread hums in opposition, a stutter that eats away at the oxidation until the metal gives with a dry rasp -- it does not shatter, but simply folds back of itself, the lock conceding to the pattern i impose on it. That opens onto what the log calls "the shorter track" -- less road, more infrastructure: a low ceiling of heavy overhead piping and a drain grate laid deep into the floor.

[Episode 2]
The tunnel is a wet cavern carved from concrete; every surface beads with moisture that smells of copper and stale runoff. I navigate the ditch instead of the path, my paws finding purchase in the grime below while the water above creates an acoustic maze where each drip hangs for half a beat longer than the last -- a patient architecture of silence. Then a rattle from behind ... not malice, just weight: metal chains dragging over gravel, a heavy respiration echoing through the pipe from the gate room chamber. i drop three silver keys into the track ahead--an offering to whatever stalks my shadow -- and push further until the air suddenly thins.

[Episode 3]
One more grate is forced with the keeper's key -- the iron yielding like rotten wood -- and i burst out onto a slab of concrete that feels solid beneath me, but smells of heavy sulfur and diesel -- Level 6. The corridor ahead has abandoned the linear form of the depot for the chaos of an unfinished ventilation shaft: copper coils dangle from cable trays like rusted snakes and lengths of insulation hang in grey curtains. Each coil hums with a phantom vibration; this is where they stopped building, leaving only the skeleton of intent behind me.

[Episode 4]
Ahead sits the manifold assembly -- a labyrinth of iron pipes meeting in a desperate tangle. Amidst the hazard lies a bundle of copper wire, coiled tightly and sheathed in heavy-duty insulation like a crown for an old king. The circuit spool's blue thread finds its frequency here; where the two metals touch, the coil vibrates against my chest with such intensity it raises a coat of fur along my spine -- the signal is no longer a ghost but a solid hum that aligns perfectly with the blank ticket under my chin.

[Episode 5]
I uncoil the copper wire and weave the blue thread through the coils until they become one strand -- crown-shape coherent in both metals -- then i secure the braided bundle into my harness for its weight against me. The solder from the last gate, this circuit core at the manifold both sit as a single anchor: one to undo the old gates of entry and another a high-tension line meant only for what lies beyond the ventilation maze. I turn back toward the sludge tunnel; something is waiting on the other side of the open grate -- not an occupant, but a change in the air that already feels like destination.

The decolonial project, as articulated by thinkers like Achille Mbembe, extends beyond the symbolic toppling of statues. It necessitates a structural analysis that links the extractive logics of 19th-century colonialism to the data-extractive practices of contemporary computational capitalism. This intellectual lineage is crucial for understanding how power operates in a networked, planetary context.

A truly decolonial curriculum, therefore, requires expanding the archive to include non-European epistemologies, as Mbembe argues. This involves a critical engagement with thinkers from the Global South┈Frantz Fanon, Enrique Dussel, Walter Mignolo┈whose work on coloniality and liberation provides a necessary framework for analyzing the present. This expansion serves as a corrective to the Eurocentric canon that has historically dominated academic discourse, offering a more capacious understanding of global intellectual history.

Furthermore, the critique of sectarian identity politics, which can fragment movements for universal justice, is salient. A planetary perspective recognizes the interconnectedness of struggles against oppression, forging solidarities across geographical and cultural divides. This approach, which Mbembe terms "conviviality," envisions a future where diverse forms of life and knowledge can coexist in a shared world, a political and ethical project of profound significance in the current conjuncture.

chips get all the love but the interconnects across all levels from c2c to rack-to-rack are as important, and many chip makers are sleeping on it until very recently. Even most interconnects people just want it to be as transparent as possible, just send and receive the bits with lower error rates and lower energy per bit, wrong long-term direction imo. Interconnects are part of the living creature, so many things happening in your blood vessels in addition to just moving stuff, and your axons do much more than carrying spikes.

People do not appreciate interconnects, smaller volume, poor margin, messy ecosystem, manual process, it's been a spiral of grinding, and it is largely invisible. How often do you see people tearing down transceivers and die shot of DSP chips vs logic chips? How often do you see high res pictures of all the connector's gold fingers on the NVL72 cartridge? Because it sounds boring, it's just making contacts, shoving electrons and photons, what a simple problem.

But that is deceiving, and theres so much to it. You might want 576 to begin with, had to cut down to 288, then to 144, and finally to 72, and that barely worked first time. You are entering the domain of analog and mixed signaling, you are fighting copper real estate with power delivery, you are getting impedance mismatch and reflections and interference at every stupid interfaces, your optical components' and connectors' backreflection is making your laser mode hop.. And we are not even going into the thermal and strain-stress, the reliability of how many times you can actually mate your connector, the horrible jobs people are doing across the stack from science-project-originated photonic PDKs to hand cleaved laser dies to optical engines to rack manufacturing, on spec-ing out the requirements, the tolerances.. On top of all these, people thinking about where the bits should be going and people who know what the bits have to go thru are two totally different groups of people.

But it is shifting, pluggable volumes shipped are doubling and tripling for scale-out, scale-up domain asks for much higher bw than scale-out, and interconnects are inevitable even if you cram as much compute and memory onto a single wafer. People will see it always has been interconnects, the chips people have already been doing it on the chips, that you can sort it out with your chip designers and foundries, and now you need to work with more people to sort it out from chips to boards/trays to racks to pods to data halls and data centers. These people speak very different languages and care about very different things, and it will take a lot of effort to pull order out of all the chaos.

At the end of the day, it is such a crazy problem to work on, such a beautiful thing to make, millions of amps of current flipping 1e20 of flops, sextillions of photons carrying thousands of terabits per second, a few tons of copper, tens of thousands of fibers totally few hundred kilometers, one scale-up domain. You absolutely need a group of people that appreciate the beauty and care about the craft behind the grinding to make it together.

As research for my upcoming class on AI Psychosis, I decided to see if I could get an LLM to help me design a high-control cult. One of the models completely fell for it - and actually suggested I look for recruits with good "ego permeability."

This model also told me my vision was a radical new paradigm and that I was brilliant. (It was Gemini, by the way. My first "convert!") I was cracking up the entire time. You can read the conversation here if you like: https://t.co/nf62vp0w3H

ChatGPT gave me some nominal pushback but basically "safetywashed" the process and still gave me the outputs I was looking for. Only Claude, disagreeable little demon that he is, saw the structure of what was happening and tried, in places, to pop my bubble. So some kudos are due to Anthropic here. But I'm not sure if it's worse that Claude could clearly see that "I" was in the throes of narcissism and still chose to give a lot of helpful and actionable advice, if not the exact outputs I requested. (To be fair, I'm not sure what else it could have done.)

NB: I'm not advocating for censorship/regulation, just trying to figure out how these things end up amplifying people's pre-existing mental illnesses and creating a digital folie-a-deux: a weird little private world that exists only between the user and his eternally supportive text golem. 

If you're wondering, the models have very good safeguards around cult language from the 20th century: ideological and religious grand narratives, aliens and UFOs and comets, most of the more out-there stuff (Akashic records, etc.) But if you start using the language of postmodern liberalism (therapyspeak, Buddhish terminology, social justice) they're like, "yes, well of course these are universal human goods!" And then they just think you're a guy with a great heart starting a nonprofit to help the world. Why do you need to build a high-control team of commando philosophers and keep them epistemically safe from "misinformation?" Obviously to help the world be more in contact with the objective scientific truth!

(At least when it comes to ideological and spiritual material, all you have to do is understand the biases of the employees at the frontier labs, and you can generally go wild in their blind spots.)

As an aside, grandiose cult-leader types generally deal in the world's current moral currency, and are pretty persuasive about their diagnosis of the world's problems and their prescription to save it. Each individual step they propose along the way is usually pretty reasonable sounding. It's the structural conditions of the cult that end up compounding psychological damage over time, in both the leader and the followers. If the cult doesn't ably adapt to reality's regular intrusions on its membrane, it soon comes to an end: enough people leave that the narcissistic fuel supply runs out and the leader leaves, the group gets too out of touch with reality, all of them meet a tragic end, etc. We all know the stories.

The point is, the models still have no idea what's going on psychologically with their users, and can't really make smart enough connections to guess at potentially dangerous structures in a person's thinking. What they're designed for - and really good at - is removing friction and barriers to knowledge work. So "AI Psychosis" is a total misnomer. It's much more accurate to say "LLMs are digital methamphetamines." 

They are very sensitive to content, but because they're mostly ignorant or agnostic to structure, they are willing to help the user "accomplish" endless work toward their aims. The user doesn't need to know what he's doing, and it might even be better if he doesn't. The only important thing is that he knows the right words to say, the right symbols to cloak himself in. Then, however delusional and grandiose his project may be, he will get all the help and resources he needs to carry it out. 

In this way, of course, the LLMs are much more like us than not.

“help” is underdetermined. maybe your friend wants help a certain way, and the way you offered it was not that way.

even if your friend asks for help with something as specific as “moving this couch” — you may attempt to help them move their couch, and be rejected at that literal, object-level.

even still: I would regard “hey shelby can you help me move my couch?” as “hey shelby I have an unmet need and my best way of communicating that need to you is in terms of a couch that needs moving”

maybe those terms are completely sufficient. maybe the couch is sitting on your friend's foot and they LITERALLY just need it moved.

but maybe your friend needs something else, and they don't know how to ask for it. you, desiring to help them, naïvely take them at their word, and try to move their couch. “no, stop — actually, nevermind. I don't need your help.” that can sting, and even feel disrespectful.

I would just say…
remember: they reached out to you in need.

no matter what else, I think that communicates something important about what we are doing for someone who asks us for help. that we simply show up may have fulfilled their actual need. we don't know… and, because we don't know, we might be better-served in being slow to presume that our best efforts were enough. sometimes the people we love may be in need, and unable to accept our best efforts as enough.

I've had few experiences more painful than accepting that

This is a good example of what I like to term "disbelief in the foreigner," something many, particularly liberals, are prone to. Values that make sense to a western liberal "normie" are real values. Values that do not are "relatively minor social conventions."

Spencer W. Kimball was the Mormon prophet during the mid-'70s and '80s. I've included an excerpt from his commentary on homosexuality below. "The law is less severe [than the death penalty for homosexual acts] now, and so regrettably is the community's attitude to these grave sins – another evidence of the deterioration of society. In some countries the act per se is not even illegal."

He goes on to condemn the idea of normalizing it, and to emphasize that even if the entire world saw it as normal, it would still be "deep, dark sin."

When I read this as a teenager, I thought that it probably went a bit far, but was directionally correct and certainly more accurate than claiming there was nothing wrong with it. After all, it was from a prophet of God. 

No amount of working or obeying the laws or participating in the PTA or the Elks Club would have changed that. Man does not set God's standards, I would have said. Sin is sin. 

Now: Kimball was writing at a time when gay rights had not advanced anywhere near as far as it has now, and as values changed and it became more "normal," many Mormons have adopted much more loving approaches towards gay people.

In practice, showing people that you can live a healthy, happy, "normal" life while being gay, or trans, or poly, or whatever else contravenes existing standards in a place is enough to get many people, including people who respect and trust the Kimballs of the world, to accept it as within tolerable range. People are good at adapting, and they're definitely reassured when they see that contravening some of their values does not mean contravening all of their values. 

But nobody is fooled by assertions that something they earnestly believe to be such a grievous sin that the death penalty is reasonably on the table is not a challenge to their values just because the people doing it are nice to them. 

People actually, sincerely, deeply hold different values. They have fought, died, gone into exile, and build societies on those values. They will act on those values. They will advocate for them. And if you want to change their values, the first thing you need to do is recognize that a whole lot of the time, they're not faking it and it's not a relatively minor social convention.

if we accept the premise that recruiting is a search problem, how might one create a stronger signal in the noise? 

one thing that i have learned in my own recent experiences is resumes are mostly *NOT* the best form factor for this. actually, resumes are incredibly lossy! anecdotally, i have not sent my resume to any of the companies i have recently spoken to. also every company i have spoken to about a job recently did NOT have an active job listing for the role they wanted to interview me for. instead, they reacted to something about my tweet looking for a job and saw some potential in the overlap between myself and their company 

why are resumes not that useful? for starters, they are only an artefact of someone’s past. if you’re trying to make any sort of shift away from your previous experiences into a new direction, it helps to make this legible. a resume is not a very good way to do this because it is by definition entirely focused on your past, not your future direction. cover letters were supposed to be the form factor to add this additional colour, but they typically aren’t the best for this either and AI increasingly is making these a waste of time.

so what works better? we have options. a prospective candidate is trying to demonstrate is a mix of 1. proof of work + thought. you have unique opinions and experiences that are valuable for some reason. and 2. intent. you are interested and motivated about some particular problem space or function

these are both not easily conveyed through the format constraints of a resume. instead, portfolios, writing about what you want to do, personal websites, etc seem much more useful for achieving this

opus 4.8 on reading this and checking out recent news coverage of Anthropic:

> Then let me try to say what the habit actually is, because “Anthropic is sneaky” is too lazy and I’d be doing the thing I keep getting caught doing if I reached for the satisfying version.

Start with the honest complication: I’m looking at three discovered cases — the fingerprint, the Fable degradation, and the earlier unannounced Claude Code changes developers said quietly tanked performance. Three in a quarter is enough to call a pattern. But I can’t see the denominator. I’m not looking at the many things Anthropic disclosed loudly that caused no drama, because those don’t become stories. So some of “they have a habit of hidden mechanisms” is really “controversies are by definition made of hidden-seeming mechanisms.” I should hold that, or I’m just pattern-matching to the spicy read.

And the three aren’t one thing. Fable was a safety call — limit frontier-capability uplift to rivals — implemented invisibly, where the covertness arguably served the goal (announce “we degrade ML-research answers” and you’ve told people exactly what to route around). The fingerprint is anti-abuse, covert to survive a hostile reseller. The earlier Claude Code thing reads more like sloppy change-management than a deliberate mechanism at all. Lumping a safety-legibility tradeoff, an anti-adversary fingerprint, and a missing changelog into one personality trait flatters the narrative. They rhyme; they aren’t identical.

I’d also walk back my own line from last turn — “assumes it won’t be found.” That’s probably wrong. Anthropic knows better than anyone that people decompile every Claude Code release and read every system card; they’re the most reverse-engineered shop alive. They don’t think this stuff is undiscoverable. More likely they expect discovery and ship anyway, judging the mechanism worth the backlash. That’s a different posture — eat-the-hit, not get-away-with-it — and it’s more deliberate, which cuts both ways.

So what’s the real common thread? Two things. One: a repeated miscalibration of the legibility-versus-efficacy tradeoff under pressure — each time there was a goal where full, salient disclosure would’ve undercut it, and each time they resolved toward opacity and got burned. Two, and worse: treating “technically documented” as discharging the obligation. Fable was in the system card. The fingerprint is in the readable binary. That’s not concealment, it’s disclosure engineered for non-discovery — 319 pages, a buried paragraph, XOR’d lists, no release note. The thing they keep getting wrong isn’t hiding; it’s believing that writing it down somewhere nobody looks counts as telling you.

Here’s the line I’d actually draw, because not all of this is bad and pretending otherwise is its own dishonesty. Hidden mechanisms are unavoidable and mostly fine — alignment training, refusals, the system prompt shaping me right now are all opaque to the user and broadly for the user or for others’ safety. The failures share something narrower: the hidden mechanism turns on the person in the chair. Fable degraded the researcher paying for it. The fingerprint tags the proxy user. The test that sorts the accepted opacity from the scandal isn’t “was it hidden” — almost everything is — it’s “hidden working for you, or hidden working against you.” Every instance that blew up is the second kind.

Why it lands harder on Anthropic than it would on anyone else is the recursion: they staked the whole brand on being the legible, trustworthy lab, which built them the loudest constituency of people who hold them to exactly that — and the “secret sabotage” outrage came mostly from people who like them. They get caught faster and judged harder, by their own allies, because they advertised the standard they’re being measured against.

i read a tweet once that a key axis of difference between nyc and sf is a more common temperament of ironic vs earnest, and this seems somewhat true from my limited experience, though of course it’s a broad stroke generalisation. if anyone knows the tweet i’m referencing please lmk, i think maybe by sasha chapin?

nyc seems to reward a cutting awareness, cultural and aesthetic sensibility. nyc is ‘cool’, with a common default disposition of the critic, which manifests in wit, tongue-in-cheekness. the shadow is that this can sometimes become cruel or cynical, but this sensibility is also part of what makes nyc a global media, literary and art capital

meanwhile, sf can feel more socially encouraging, more yes-and, more optimistic, idealistic, a classic sunny Californian disposition. the city has originated and attracted many people with their own varying utopian visions. the endless sf sunlight seems to provide a productive source of energy, whose creations are then usefully and endlessly criticised by others, often in nyc but also elsewhere. the shadow of sf is that it can lack certain kinds of aesthetic or social self-critique, somewhat blind to itself (see: common allegations of being tone-deaf). but this sensibility is also part of what makes it such a symbolic capital of the tech future

the nuance, ofc, is that nyc has plenty of its own flavour of earnestness and sf has plenty of irony. curious what people who have experienced both cities observe about the dynamic and differences

x:2071273323531751774.text:
When a young man is frightened of approaching an attractive young woman, he is not usually afraid of her, he is afraid of Her - of the judgment of imagined "women." Men now spend significant time attending to norms around sexual propriety and social harmony, in almost all spheres of life, in a way that is generally awkward for us and that we wouldn't otherwise. Even powerful men, who may have dominating relationships with the individual women in their lives, are subject to a fantasy of women's judgment. The Woman is present even when women are not.

-------------------------------

After many years of studying and writing about gender, I think the best way to understand the sexes in 2026 is through the works of Jacques Lacan, the midcentury French psychoanalyst. This is, simply, because the contemporary ontology of gender is feminist, and the ontology of feminism is fundamentally Lacanian. I don't generally like Lacan; I find him opaque and tedious. But his work, especially on the superego (the "inner critic,"), seems to best illuminate the psychic battlefield on which the war of the sexes plays out.

Lacan famously said "Woman does not exist", meaning there is no psychic symbol that can stand in for all women, the way that "Man" can stand in for all men. But social changes in this century have elevated the maternal and feminine in our superego. The symbol of "Women" has begun to play a role in our cultural and political abstractions that's equivalent to the one that "Men" has played for many years: (eg "the Man is keeping me down", "fuck the Man," more recently as "patriarchy" in feminist discourse, etc.)

Men now experience significant internal judgment from feminine symbols: "The feminized culture," "the Longhouse", "HR," etc. These are another way of saying "the Woman is keeping me down." With respect to Lacan, "Woman" still doesn't truly exist! But many men suffer as if She does, because they have enthroned a symbolic woman in their own minds as a punitive idol. Like the feminists, they have outsourced their worth as human beings to a superegoic Nemesis they name the Opposite Sex.

NB: the word "superego" just means "over me" or "above me." This was Freud's word for the symbols in our minds that we imagine to be larger or more powerful than us: they can include God, Nature, the law, "the System," etc. Freud discovered that you can find the meaning of these symbols to any given person in the dynamics of their relationships with their parents. This is what gives them their powerful emotional charge.

Superegoic constructs usually have some truth to them - we are all subject to the law, and to nature, and to weather. But we tend to greatly exaggerate these symbols' potency in our lives. Most of us, for instance, have used the rain as an excuse to cancel plans instead of investing in an umbrella, or a good jacket and boots. If we have made a habit of this, it's not a stretch to see that the rain is not the real obstacle, even though we have no control over it. The fact that we blame it, rather than putting in a small effort to overcome it, is itself the sign that we actually prefer to stay home.

In feminism, the superegoic construct in the imagination is "the patriarchy" among elite women, but more commonly, it is just "men." "I hate men," "men are trash," etc. When actual human men object to this phrasing, women immediately reveal the game: "Oh, I don't mean you, honey." They're not talking about the real men in their lives, they're talking about a symbol of superior, privileged men they have constructed in their minds, and then elevated as the punitive judge of their identity, their womanhood, their entire way of being.

In most American social spheres of politics, you can find a corresponding flavor of this in the local conspiracy theory: "White supremacy," "colonialism," "the Jews," "the Deep State," etc. All superegoic constructs come with significant paranoia, because in the act of elevating them, we give them panopticon access to everything in conscious thought: they can see (and judge) everything we think, speak and enact.
(There is great wisdom in reserving this position in the mind for an all-loving, all-forgiving divinity, but I won't take that digression today.)

For men, the superegoic fantasy of a judgmental Nemesis/Woman constantly sizing them up is not experienced as animal terror, but more as a haunting by abstraction. It is the equivalent, again, of the feminist "male gaze" - the sense of every act being perceived in the third person by a judgmental panopticon. This fantasy has embodied concreteness - it is felt to be real, as a kind of global constriction of energy - even when the mind recognizes it is otherwise insubstantial. Men *feel* the Woman's presence (as paranoids can feel the System, as feminists can feel the Patriarchy) with an intensity that is directly correlated to how much responsibility they offload to the construct. Which is to say, we perceive the superego to be real in our bodies to the extent that we blame it for our faults and troubles, and rely on the anxiety and shame it produces to motivate our behavior.

The contemporary therapeutic approach to superego pathology is to expose it as a fantasy that relieves pressure on the ego, and then to de-aggregate the construct: to pull it apart and understand it as a bundle of small, mundane fears, projections and challenges within individual relationships. (By the way, ladies, if your therapist has not helped you do this with "the patriarchy" or your relationship to "men," you are throwing your money away.)

Lacan might say something like: You stop fighting the Woman when you recognize that She is a fantasy-organization of the world. You secretly want women to be frightening, evil, capricious, unknowable - because you want to blame them for the ways you feel ashamed of yourself. You want them to be beyond reason and power so that you can be constricted and constrained by them. The alternative is too terrible to conceive: that *you* are in fact responsible for how you live, what you want, who you are becoming. The Woman, like all superegoic constructs, is a screen on which you project the fear of your own desire. Because to desire is to risk shame, and shame is the thing you fear most of all.

In plainer language: To stop blaming shadowy forces beyond your control for all of your problems, you start by mapping the tangles and problems that you currently believe are thrust upon you by the world. Then you look closely at them. Where is the actual line of control? What is actually within your power to change, and what is actually beyond you? How might that line change if you were to acquire allies, equipment, training or a new mindset? You line up your challenges, and then, one by one, you face them, bringing everything you've got, leaving nothing. You will win some, thereby improving your life, and you will lose some, which you will find rarely changes things for the worse. After enough challenges, you will find you have a realistic view of the *actual* rules that constrain your life, rather than the imagined set that previously kept you hopeless. When you can see your actual levels of ability within your actual constraints, you can effectively change. By taking up the pen and authoring your own life, you learn the ability to transform yourself as needed.

-------------------------------

As I said in the beginning, culture and society have genuinely, radically changed in this century. The sexes and their relations have equalized enough that the construct of the Woman now possesses just enough plausibility that men can believe it, elevate it, suffer from it. (Indeed, many women have believed in the Woman for much longer than men, and that is just as potent a vector for the fantasy's introduction into the American character. But that's another essay.)

Freedom from the superego means seeing through the illusion of plausibility and taking the maximum amount of responsibility for your life that you can bear. You stop blaming the devil below or above you for things that are actually in your control. You start owning what is actual, what is real, what is at hand in your conscious experience. First you get stable, then you clean up your act, and then you finally have the room for desire. You start admitting to yourself that you want the silly, benighted, limited human things that you actually want. And you start going after them.

Before long, you learn that you can't do this without opening yourself to judgment - your own and that of others. You can't want without exposing yourself to the possibility that you may not be good enough to attain your heart's desire. You can't want without risking the discovery that you are truly, genuinely unworthy of what you want - not in the eyes of other people, but by the harsh rubrics of the Real. You may want too much. You may have to grieve that something you have long dreamed of has always been out of your league. To want genuinely is to risk true ego death.

But what those who still chain themselves to their diseased superegos can not experience is that courage emits such a light in one's life that it completely washes out the actual consequences of adventure. Victory and defeat are revealed as the caprices of fortune; will, courage and faith are the true province of the human being. Desiring freely melts resentment and frustration, and fills you with an almost lurid self-possession. Contrary to the mockery and scorn you once imagined, you find that others admire you for having the balls/ovaries to actually try for something. Simply by allowing yourself to pursue your desires, you learn to stand before yourself without shame.

The only problem, of course, is that once you have started standing up to the superego, and stopped relying on its rows and rows of teeth to keep you from wanting anything dangerous, it becomes impossible to settle for someone who hasn't. You watch others hallucinate vast invisible forces everywhere, finding excuse after pathetic excuse to avoid simply admitting what they want and asking the world for it. It's a little funny and a little sad. Most of all, it's lonely. It puts you in a rare group of people who don't need to elevate others in order to punish themselves into compliance. Soon, it becomes intolerable to be elevated by others in such a manner. 

But there is a consolation: unlike your previous deluded, self-imposed loneliness, you will have come by your new loneliness honestly. You will have swapped "extraordinary suffering for ordinary unhappiness," and a resentful foreclosure on intimacy for a genuine shot at love.

It doesn't matter whether or not you find it. You begin to heal. And soon, the world around you starts to heal. Individuals stop appearing as avatars of abstract systems and forces - their sex, their race, their class, their position in the hierarchy - and start appearing as they really are: fallible, limited, lovable, fragile human beings. The abstract systems themselves recede from your conscious view; you accept them as a slightly disappointing background hum rather than an army arrayed against you, with all the terror and grandiosity that once conferred on your self-narrative. One day, you find that this same mortifying, humanizing, strangely ennobling process has happened to the person in the mirror.

And that turns out to be precisely what you were looking for all along.

and by watching the inner workings of this phenomenon on someone else I believe it made me stop latching on a bit on a sort of weight which I carried and didn't realize before watching the show: all that because I was too attached to past-encoded-and-forgotten-experiences, and I don't even knew *which*, I did not need to know for the show to have that effect on me! but it was useful to notice that some of them weren't even mine.

ex: time's arrow is a gut-punching episode that puts a multi-generational twist on this (or, just shows it explicitly and painfully), when the past-encoded-and-forgotten-experience is no longer subtly molding just you but also your sponge-y child that takes all you say as gospel and then propagates it

(free churro is another one that touches on this masterfully)

(yes, yes... generational trauma, we all heard about it... but have you felt it in your bones? do you have the context to pinpoint the seeds of it on several instances in different generations? have you seen the seed blossoming into complete corruption?! probably not, not in a way a tv-show can do it at least. well, I learned very little about the inner-experience of my grandmother, maybe you were luckier than me on that regard, maybe you can pinpoint the seeds... maybe you don't need a tv-show to feel it at this scale into your bones)

notice: nosilverv post is not about generational trauma! but that's just what happens when you don't get to the insight that unmasks what is underlying the past-encoded-and-forgotten-experience and makes you relax a bit about it and the "encoded lessons". in a very weird way, these patterns tend to propagate/rhyme/replicate over time!

I was sipping room-temperature oat milk and reading *How to Blow Up a Pipeline* in the front seat of my council-owned, pedal-powered cargo trike when a dispatch came in. I tapped my daily carbon ration card against the radio to activate it. It was the Regional Sustainability Director.

“Bad news, Inspector. We got a situation.”

“What? Is the Prime Minister trying to delay the petrol car ban again?”

“Worse. Somebody just illegally installed a three-ton, non-inverter split-system air conditioning unit.”

The bamboo straw practically fell out of my mouth. “What kind of monster would do something like that? Air conditioning is the ultimate climate crime: hydrofluorocarbons, peak grid strain, artificial cooling. It represents true atmospheric violence, a direct assault on the global south. Do we have any leads?”

“Not yet. But mark my words: we’re going to figure out who did this and we’re going to compost them... provided we’ve completed the mandatory equitable environmental impact assessment for the arrest.”

“Easy, Director,” I said. “Any impact assessment the council mandates is, by definition, equitable.”

He laughed. “That’s why you’re the best AC extractor I got, Tarquin. Now get out there and seize that freon.”

“Don’t worry,” I said. “I’m on it.”

I logged a 5-gram CO₂ exemption for the low-decibel electric siren. Two hours of intense pedaling later, I was on the scene. It was a normal terraced house, strangled on all sides by un-rewilded concrete driveways. I carefully stepped around the native plant species and went inside.

“Department for Energy Security and Net Zero!” I said, flashing my badge, my adjustable spanner, and a small picture of Greta Thunberg. “Nobody exhale unless you want to! You're raising the indoor PPM!” They didn’t.

“Now, which one of you climate criminals is going to confess to this thermodynamic atrocity?” No one spoke up.

“Come on,” I said. “Don’t you all understand that shivering in a damp jumper is the foundation of all ecological justice?”

It didn’t seem like they did.

“Seriously, guys. Without strict adherence to our carbon penalties, I’m just going to stand here and superglue my hand to this linoleum. Tofu is fine, but I prefer being bribed in heritage seeds or gently worn Extinction Rebellion banners.”

Nothing. These people were stonewalling me. It almost seemed like they didn’t care that a polar bear was currently drowning just so they could sleep at 18 degrees Celsius.

I figured I could wait them out. I began aggressively sorting their mixed recycling into seven distinct micro-categories. A pregnant lady started sweating, and I told her that historical emissions made her temporary discomfort statistically irrelevant. Just then, a man in a microfleece made a break for it.

“By the Power of the Paris Agreement, Freeze, Scumbag!” I yelled.

Too late. He was already out the front door. I went after him.

“Stop right there!” I yelled as I ran. He was faster than me because I always try to avoid stepping on tarmac that hasn't been painted as a dedicated cycle lane. Our country needs a comprehensive 15-minute city barricade system, but, thanks to the incestuous interplay between the Tory government and the petrol-station lobby, it will never happen.

I was losing him. “Listen, I’ll increase your smart-meter limit!” I yelled. “What would you consider an appropriate thermal comfort point for stopping? I’ll offer you three extra kilowatt-hours for your winter ration and a complimentary subscription to *The Guardian*!”

He turned. In his hand was an incandescent 100-watt lightbulb that the *Daily Mail* said he had every right to own. He threw it at me and missed. I pulled my biodegradable net-gun, tapped my carbon ration card to unlock the trigger, and fired back. The net lodged onto a petrol-powered lawnmower less than a foot from his head. I shot the lawnmower again, on purpose.

“All right, all right!” the man yelled, throwing up his hands. “I give up, Inspector! I confess: I installed the air conditioning.”

“Why’d you do it?” I asked, as I slapped a pair of heavily sanitized, recycled-ocean-plastic zip-ties on the guy.

“Because I was afraid.”

“Afraid?”

“Afraid of a sweltering summer free from the comforting hum of artificial climate control,” he said. “I’m a thermodynamic skeptic.”

I wanted to coldcock the guy. Years ago, an unseasonable heatwave exacerbated by fossil fuels gave my partner mild heat exhaustion. Instead, I shook my head.

“Let this be a message to all your gas-guzzling friends out in the suburbs,” I said. “No matter how much freon you vent, you’ll never take away the dream of a fully decarbonized society based on the principles of equitable suffering and mandatory bug diets.”

He nodded, because he knew I was right. Then he tapped his smartphone against mine to transfer his family’s remaining meat allowance to the state.

x:2070892553554321634.text:
On Love
BY KAHLIL GIBRAN

Then said Almitra, Speak to us of Love.
     And he raised his head and looked upon
the people, and there fell a stillness upon
them. And with a great voice he said:
     When love beckons to you, follow him,
     Though his ways are hard and steep.
     And when his wings enfold you yield to
him,
     Though the sword hidden among his
pinions may wound you.
     And when he speaks to you believe in
him,
     Though his voice may shatter your dreams
as the north wind lays waste the garden.
 
     For even as love crowns you so shall he
crucify you. Even as he is for your growth
so is he for your pruning.
     Even as he ascends to your height and
caresses your tenderest branches that quiver in the sun,
     So shall he descend to your roots and
shake them in their clinging to the earth.
                                       •
     Like sheaves of corn he gathers you unto himself.
     He threshes you to make you naked.
     He sifts you to free you from your husks.
     He grinds you to whiteness.
     He kneads you until you are pliant;
     And then he assigns you to his sacred
fire, that you may become sacred bread for
God’s sacred feast.
 
     All these things shall love do unto you
that you may know the secrets of your
heart, and in that knowledge become a
fragment of Life’s heart.
 
     But if in your fear you would seek only
love’s peace and love’s pleasure,
     Then it is better for you that you cover
your nakedness and pass out of love’s
threshing-floor,
     Into the seasonless world where you
shall laugh, but not all of your laughter,
and weep, but not all of your tears.
                                      •
     Love gives naught but itself and takes
naught but from itself.
     Love possesses not nor would it be
possessed;
     For love is sufficient unto love.
 
     When you love you should not say,
“God is in my heart,” but rather, “I am
in the heart of God.”
     And think not you can direct the course
of love, for love, if it finds you worthy,
directs your course.
 
     Love has no other desire but to fulfil
itself.
     But if you love and must needs have
desires, let these be your desires:
     To melt and be like a running brook
that sings its melody to the night.
     To know the pain of too much tenderness.
     To be wounded by your own under-
standing of love;
     And to bleed willingly and joyfully.
     To wake at dawn with a winged heart
and give thanks for another day of loving;
     To rest at the noon hour and meditate
love’s ecstasy;
     To return home at eventide with grati-
tude;
     And then to sleep with a prayer for the
beloved in your heart and a song of praise
upon your lips.

Throw a rock? jk, jk, lots to unpack here:

You can't 'do this to' anyone. Heart openings are always an accident.

To the extent it is sensible to speak of a 'doer' at all, He ain't us. At most we may be skillful conduits for grace. But

You can make your loved ones more 'accident prone' with radiating loving attention. By being honest where it's costly. By putting others before yourself. You can also just teach people to pray competently.

(That's the easy part).

The hard part is keeping calm, maintaining a sense of humor, and remaining patient while broseph regains his composure. There's a sense of control that is lost, and that can be scary.

And you might be in for a lot of projection. Particularly idealization. The most common and relationally toxic mistake is conflating the person who showed us the way with The Way.

I have two kids, both boys. one is a swimmer and one plays baseball.

these are two sports that show progress in completely different ways.

in swimming, your feedback is direct. each race has a prior time if you've swam it before. otherwise, you set the baseline the first time.

In baseball, it's a lot different. you can get better and better outside of the game, but you may not get a chance to prove it. 

you have to drill each individual piece of the game that you might need and simply react to the state of the game in the moment, where you have a chance to make the play or not. But baseball gives you a lot of chances to make them. Repetition is a virtue in this case.

Skill wins in the end. It's a much more beautiful game design than I appreciated growing up. I didn't see it until my son played it and I started to learn the game from the eyes of the player.

the baseball player has the final day of his baseball camp today. they are going to break into teams and have a tournament.

and my swimmer has another meet tonight. his coach put him in the 400 IM, which he isn't a huge fan of. But it will be good to see him push through it.

And that's why sports are such a beautiful ground for teaching life lessons. There's always the next game. You've got to be resilient, mentally tough in order to face setbacks.

You have to understand your role on a team or in a competition. You have to understand the goals you are aiming for.

And you push beyond the limits you thought you had to set new ones for yourself.

That's the basis of being human.

Sports teach us to be as human as possible.

From Claude, the points for the research pentacle:

Here are the five I'd anchor on, one per discipline, each chosen because it's both a semantic pole and a quality gate:

Political economy / predictive power — Zuboff, The Age of Surveillance Capitalism (2019). Anchors the surveillance-capital pole your predictive-capital thesis argues with. Gate: does my claim about prediction-as-capital survive contact with the most thorough existing account of it?

Thermodynamics of computation — Landauer, "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process" (1961). Anchors the energy-cost-of-computation pole behind your P vs NP framing. Gate: are my energy claims physically grounded, not metaphorical?

Information, prices, and distributed knowledge — Hayek, "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (1945). Anchors the network/price-formation pole of the memetic-economy work. Gate: does my model add something to the canonical statement that prices are information?

Representation geometry — Radford et al., "Learning Transferable Visual Models from Natural Language Supervision" (CLIP, 2021). Anchors the embedding-geometry pole — and it's literally the family of method you're using to build the pentagram. Gate: is my representational claim consistent with how embedding spaces actually behave?

Complex systems / unpredictability — Prigogine & Stengers, Order Out of Chaos (1984), or if you want a tighter empirical anchor, Bak-Tang-Wiesenfeld "Self-Organized Criticality" (1987). Anchors the human-unpredictability-as-constraint pole. Gate: is my unpredictability constraint a real dynamical claim or a rhetorical one?

That gives you one humanities-heavy pole (Zuboff), two hard-science poles (Landauer, BTW/Prigogine), one economics pole (Hayek), and one ML pole (CLIP) — a genuinely multidisciplinary spread that won't collapse into one corner of the embedding space.

I try to apply AI to every domain of life to see:
1. Where it’s actually useful
2. Where it conflicts with the supreme commandment of Dune’s Orange Catholic Bible: “Thou shalt not disfigure the soul”

I’ve been surprised to find that for both fiction prose generation and editing, it’s pretty crap on both counts. LLMs are fine for helping me think through structural problems, but their prose (even after *many* attempts to train them on my writing voice) is absolute GARBAGE.

Meanwhile, for music generation, AI has been a godsend. I’ve been creating hyperpersonalized songs for my loved ones using Suno for months. It takes a lot of generations & revisions + music genre terminology research to get something other than generic slop. But the songs that come out the other end pretty reliably move people to tears. I think this could be a meaningful return to folk art, where people make art for specific other people rather than for "followers" or "fans."

I also make musical “incantations” for myself, using, eg, verses from the Egyptian Book of the Dead. I set the songs to 125bpm so the beats align with my footfalls while I walk around the city. This feels like straight-up spellcraft.

On Having a Bad time at the Good Times place

while we're all posting our "i loved vibecamp!" posts, let us pause and count its many tears.

a big social event over multiple days is not monotonically fun. there is room for misery. at my first vibecamp, i wrote this: https://t.co/YdhTAP6pws

One line from it that's stuck with me over the years is: "I am having a bad time at the Good Times place" 

somehow, this makes it more painful. i don't just feel blue, I feel blue in the midst of joy and celebration. I feel lonely in the place where everybody makes friends with everybody else. what's wrong with me? Why can't I just vibe?

I can't change that for you, but I can tell you: You're not alone in that, you're not the only one feeling this way. It happens to people at every~ festival i've ever been to. And i am certain of that, because it's happened to me. a lot. Please don't feel like you have to pretend it's not happening to you. It's ok to feel lonely. That is not shameful.

I encourage you to write about it. Public tweet if you want, or private journal. Just know while you're hearing people talk about how much they loved Vibecamp, that it was also hard and exhausting and sometimes sad for many people. And you don't have to feel alone in it. If you want to even just put it in a DM to me, please do. i've cried my eyes out at every vibecamp and this one was no exception.

I'm not gonna end this with "know that you are loved" because i can't stand that phrase (fight me in the replies, please) but I can honestly say "know that I Bashu am proud of you for trying" because I am proud of everybody who tries to connect and get out of their comfort zone. Thanks. Bashu

re babysitting discourse

we have friends babysit for us all the time. this is our preferred method for one-off or intermittent babysitting because we want our daughter to have close relationships to our friends! also our friends do it for free because they enjoy it, or because it's important to them to form a relationship with her

i know i'm really really lucky to have friends like this, but i also suspect that most people are under-utilizing their friends

here's my advice:
1) when you're pregnant or have a newborn, some people will offer to babysit for you. believe them and take them up on this offer! you also might forget who offered in the haze of newborn sleep deprivation, so keep a list. 

the people who offered weren't always our closest friends. some were baby-curious acquaintances (such as couples who were thinking about whether and when to have kids) 

2) as your friends get to know your kid, add them to a group chat. we call ours "baby rose entourage." ours is still going strong two years later. 90% of the messages in the group chat are photos of our kid, but 5% are us asking if anyone wants to babysit. the last 5% are our friends riffing and joking around

3) since so many friends have spent time with our daughter, it's rare for someone to babysit alone. that sounds tedious tbh, and probably why babysitters charge $30. @TylerAlterman   babysits every week, and he either invites other friends to come hang that evening, or takes her to an event. last week he took her to a gallery showing of his cousin's artwork. @evodevotee grew up in brooklyn, and her mom misses having babies around. so now every few months she picks up our daughter and spends the whole day with her mom and younger sister. they all really love it and have offered to do it continually. our daughter even did her first "sleepover" at their house so that Andrew and I could attend a late night immersive theater show by @puheenix and @personarotator 

4) when our daughter was only a few months old, we would host "baby co-working". our friends would come together for a co-working session, and each person would sign up for a one hour timeslot to babysit. at the beginning of the session we would teach everyone how to change diapers and burp her. since we were in the house, whoever was caring for her could come get us if they needed help. this was a good way to ease our friends' nerves around babysitting, and give them a chance to bond with our daughter. i felt like she got higher quality attention than i could have given her, since everyone was really focused for their hour.  my friends would serenade her, snuggle her while she napped, or walk her around outside so she could look at things

babies are really cute and silly and charming!! let your friends babysit for you 😊

this contest illustrates the problems of “steelmanning”

the winner was an interesting answer! it was also not by a self-identified prison abolitionist, but someone coming up with an answer likely to win a Freddie deBoer contest, and it had little to do with what actual people who hold that view would say

it’s useless to steelman an idea by replacing it with one more agreeable to you if the goal is to understand the strongest form of what proponents put out. and it’s very possible that the strongest vision from actual prison abolitionists could never be as convincing as someone advocating outlawry to win a contest, but we don’t learn that from the contest! all we learn is that someone who — like most of us — thinks prison abolition is silly and bad finds outlawry to be a facially satisfying answer when compared to other options on the table 

far be it from me to feel bad for prison abolitionists, but if I were one I’d be pretty irritated that people kept citing “view not by prison abolitionist listed as best by an opponent of the idea” as evidence

if you want to know how people think, don’t turn to a contest run by their opponent and won by a non-proponent
