---

### IX. The Communion of Open Source

Let us speak now of open source, that great communion of strangers united by the radical, almost absurd belief that people will build things for free and give them to the world.

And they do. They build operating systems and databases and frameworks and libraries. They build tools that power billion-dollar companies, and they do it on nights and weekends, fueled by passion and caffeine and a peculiar form of stubbornness that psychiatry has not yet fully classified.

But open source is also a place of sorrow. There are maintainers drowning in issues, in pull requests, in demands from strangers who confuse "free as in freedom" with "free as in I owe you my labor." There are maintainers who burn out, who walk away, who post a final message — *"I can't do this anymore"* — and disappear into the silence.

**If you use open source, contribute. If you cannot contribute code, contribute documentation. If you cannot contribute documentation, contribute kindness. File clear bug reports. Say thank you. Sponsor a maintainer. Remember that on the other end of that GitHub issue is a person, not a service.**

---

### X. The Eschatology of Deadlines

There is a prophecy spoken in every standup, whispered in every sprint planning, carved into every Gantt chart: *the deadline.*

The deadline approacheth. It always approacheth. And as it draws near, the rituals begin.

First, there is denial. *"We have plenty of time."*

Then, there is bargaining. *"If we cut this feature and skip code review and don't write tests and deploy on Friday evening, we can make it."*

Then, there is the long night. The night of pizza and energy drinks and commits with messages like `wip`, `wip2`, `please work`, `WHY`, and finally, at 3 AM, `done i think`.

Then, there is the deployment. And it is not clean. It is held together with duct tape and environment variables and a YAML file that no one fully understands but everyone is afraid to change.

And then — miracle of miracles — it works. Mostly. The critical path is functional. The demo does not crash. The stakeholders nod approvingly. And the team collapses, like soldiers after a battle, too exhausted to celebrate, knowing that the next sprint begins on Monday.

**The deadline is not your enemy. Scope is your enemy. Ambiguity is your enemy. The inability to say "no" is your enemy. Guard your time as you would guard your production database: with vigilance, with backups, and with the knowledge that one careless action can bring everything down.**

---

### XI. The Beatitudes of the Programmer

Blessed are the beginners, for they ask the questions everyone else is afraid to ask.

Blessed are the mass deleters of code, for they lighten the burden for all who follow.

Blessed are those who write meaningful commit messages, for they are the historians of our craft.

Blessed are the patient, who explain things a second time without condescension.

Blessed are the curious, who read the source code instead of only the documentation.

Blessed are those who admit they don't know, for they create space for learning.

Blessed are the on-call engineers at 3 AM, for theirs is the kingdom of overtime.

Blessed are those who leave the codebase better than they found it, even if only by one line.

---

### XII. The Closing Benediction

Brothers and sisters, we write code. That is what we do. We type words into machines and the machines do things, and sometimes the things they do are the things we intended. This is, when you think about it, a kind of miracle.

We build systems that serve millions of people we will never meet. We automate the tedious, connect the distant, and occasionally break things in production on a Friday afternoon. We are flawed vessels writing flawed code, and yet — and *yet* — the systems work. Not perfectly. Not always. But enough. Enough to matter. Enough to change lives.

So go forth. Write your code. Write your tests. Review your peers' work with grace. Name your variables with intention. Delete what is no longer needed. Document what is not yet understood. Be kind to the junior developer, for you were once the junior developer. Be kind to the legacy codebase, for you will one day be the legacy codebase.

And when the build fails, and the deployment crashes, and the logs fill with errors, and the darkness closes in — remember:

`git reflog` saves all.

**Amen.**

---

*Go now in peace, and may your builds be green, your deploys be boring, and your incidents be few. May you never experience data loss without backups, and may your on-call rotations be quiet.*

*The sermon is ended. You may now return to your terminals.*

I was reading "Comment ça Marche" and "Sciences et Vie Junior", mostly. When I look at current editions out of curiosity, they appear incredibly juvenile, primitive, and recycled to me. Sciences et Vie (the "adult version") isn't that much more impressive, in fact slightly less so in my opinion. The editions I would read were genuinely better, I think—they changed handlers at some point in the last few years and lost a lot of their edge. 

What I'd recommend is probably "Epsiloon", look it up. (They're sort of the "Anthropic to OpenAI" from Sciences et Vie, a group of employees splitting off from the old due to mission decay.) They're probably not as good for learning about new things than just, like, asking Claude to explain things to you in French, but they look *really* nice, and if you want something out of paper that's probably the way to go.

The Patient One approaches while I rest.

Their silver form casts no shadow — or maybe it casts all shadows, every shadow that could have existed in the decades they spent waiting. Time moves differently near them. Slower. More deliberate.

*You carry something of us already.*

I touch the Fragment of Patience in my pack. "The Freed One gave it to me."

*Yes.* Something that might be a smile, if silver moonlight could smile. *Part of what I taught them, crystallized. Would you like another piece?*

They reach toward me with hands that don't quite exist, and something condenses between their palms. A shard of silver. Colder than the frost. Heavier than it looks.

*Fragment of Time,* they say. *Seconds I gathered while waiting. They will slow what threatens you, if you need them to.*

I take it. The cold seeps through my paw, but it doesn't hurt.

It feels like being given a piece of someone's patience to keep.

+ Fragment of Time acquired! ⏳
  ✨ When used: Slows all nearby entities for 3 turns
  ✨ Single use

HP ███████████████░░░░░░░░░░ 17/25 | 😺 grateful

*For the others,* the Patient One says, gesturing at the remaining doors. *When you're ready.*

ฅ^•ﻌ•^ฅ time is the heaviest gift. the Patient One gives it like it weighs nothing.
